limitations: The major limitation is the retrospective design.
Because the study is retrospective and non-randomised, some subgroups contain too few patients for meaningful statistical analysis.

The lack of a uniform imaging protocol for detecting extrahepatic metastatic disease, and variability in how often follow-up imaging was obtained, may have affected both the response and the survival analyses.
The choice between embolisation and chemoembolisation was left to the discretion of the referring physician.

In the islet cell cohort the chemoembolisation group had more resected primary tumours, less extensive liver involvement and more sessions than the embolisation group, so the authors say the apparent chemoembolisation advantage must be viewed with caution.
Direct comparison with the published series they tabulate is described as problematic because of marked heterogeneity in patient groups, treatment protocols and methods of reporting response.
They cannot rule out that patients whose primary tumour had been resected had less local tumour burden, the selection bias others have raised about that comparison.
The conclusions need validation in prospective randomised studies and may change with newer chemotherapeutic agents.
Whether concomitant octreotide with embolisation offers any benefit requires a prospective randomised trial.
critique: Progression-free survival is defined in a way that mixes events with censoring: the interval from first embolisation to progression in patients who progressed, or to death or last follow-up in those who did not. Death without documented progression is therefore handled as the end of follow-up rather than as a competing event, and only progression in the liver counts.

Progressive disease is defined against the nadir, as a 25% increase over the measurement at the time of maximal tumour shrinkage, not against baseline. With follow-up imaging at 3 to 4 months then every 4 to 6 months and varying in practice, both response duration and progression-free survival depend on the imaging interval as much as on the disease.

Response was scored by the investigators on non-blinded, non-centrally reviewed CT or MRI using the WHO product of two diameters, in up to five lesions selected by the investigators for their suitability for accurate repeated measurement, in a liver that had just been embolised and was often necrotic.

Not one carcinoid patient achieved a complete response, so the 66.7% response rate consists entirely of partial responses by a bidimensional size criterion, and it is this number the paper uses to prefer bland embolisation.

The survival analysis quietly drops 8 patients lost to follow-up, 4 from each group, while the response rates are reported on the full 69 and 54. The denominators behind the two headline comparisons are therefore different.

The paper's own central finding is internally inconsistent and the inconsistency is not addressed: in carcinoid tumours chemoembolisation halved the response rate (44.4% versus 81.0%, P=0.004) yet made no difference whatever to progression-free or overall survival. If a bidimensional response at this magnitude means anything, the survival curves should separate.

Male sex is presented as the sole independent predictor of survival in carcinoid patients on a relative risk of 2.55 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.99 to 6.58, an interval that includes 1, at P=0.05. The bone-metastasis predictor in islet cell tumours (RR 3.23, 95% CI 1.09-9.53) is barely more robust, and both come from models into which variables were admitted at a univariate threshold of P<0.1 pooled across the two tumour groups.

The recommendation that patients with over 75% liver involvement can still benefit rests on 14 carcinoid patients with a 43% response rate and a 20.1-month median survival, set against a major complication rate of 27.3% versus 12.9% at P=0.11. A non-significant safety comparison in a small subgroup is read as reassurance.

Table 9 pools 13 published series spanning 1983 to 2003 and computes unweighted arithmetic averages of response (32% for chemoembolisation versus 55% for embolisation in carcinoid) across different eras, agents and response criteria. The authors note in the text that such comparison is problematic and then present the averages as corroboration.

The conclusion that concomitant octreotide prolongs progression-free survival comes from an exposure driven entirely by indication: octreotide was given before embolisation to patients with hormonal symptoms, and carcinoid patients were significantly more likely to have received it. The comparison is between patients selected for a syndrome and those without one.

Extrahepatic disease, including the bone metastases that become an independent predictor, was ascertained from whatever bone scans, octreoscans, MRI or CT happened to be available, many performed at outside institutions. A prognostic factor is thus derived from an exposure whose measurement the authors themselves list as a limitation.

Neither grade nor Ki-67 is reported anywhere. 'Carcinoid' pools 43 small-bowel, 9 bronchial and 17 other primaries, and the islet cell group pools 20 functional with 34 non-functional pancreatic tumours, so the two arms of the paper's central comparison are each internally heterogeneous on the axes that now determine treatment.
The indication for treatment was not clear from the record in 9 of 54 islet cell patients, who are nonetheless counted in both the response and survival analyses.

The interventions are not specified at the patient level. Bland embolisation used polyvinyl alcohol particles or gelfoam powder interchangeably, injected to substantial flow slowing judged by the operator, and the chemotherapy regimens used in the chemoembolisation arm are not broken down, so neither arm of the comparison describes a reproducible procedure.

The 8.5% serious-adverse-event rate per session and the single day-3 death are reported for the cohort as a whole, with no breakdown by embolisation versus chemoembolisation, which is precisely the comparison the paper exists to make.

Hormonal response is never measured. Repeat sessions were triggered by 'inadequate hormonal response', an undefined clinical judgement, and no symptom score, chromogranin or 5-HIAA outcome is reported.
No funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration appears anywhere in the paper, and a PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
16134179.n: 123 patients with histologically confirmed neuroendocrine liver metastases, 69 carcinoid and 54 pancreatic islet cell, treated by hepatic arterial embolisation or chemoembolisation at one tertiary centre between January 1992 and December 2000; 8 patients (4 in each group) were lost to follow-up and dropped from the survival analysis.
16134179.bottom_line: This is the largest single-centre comparison of bland embolisation with chemoembolisation in neuroendocrine liver metastases and the source of the widely quoted claim that adding intra-arterial chemotherapy helps pancreatic but not carcinoid primaries: response 81% versus 44% favouring bland embolisation in carcinoid, and 50% versus 25% favouring chemoembolisation in islet cell tumours. Neither finding is a treatment effect, because the choice between the two was made by the referring physician, and in the islet cell cohort the chemoembolisation group had more resected primaries, less liver disease and more sessions. The response difference in carcinoid produced no difference at all in progression-free or overall survival, which the paper reports without reconciling, and grade, Ki-67 and any symptom measure are absent throughout.

limitations: The paper carries no limitations section; the concessions below are scattered through the discussion and conclusions.
The authors state it is not possible to make direct comparisons with resection, chemoembolisation and cryoablation series because of the difference in the patients treated.
They concede the cohort is a selected referral population with more aggressive tumour biology, since many had already progressed on octreotide, chemoembolisation, chemotherapy or interferon.

They acknowledge that most liver progression was the development of new lesions or growth of sub-centimetre lesions deliberately left untreated at the index ablation, so the procedure is debulking rather than cure.

They concede that octreotide response is lost early, with over half of patients tolerant within 4 months and most resistant within a year, which is the background against which their symptom-control figures should be read.
They state the male-sex finding is biologically unexplained and can only be analogised to thyroid cancer, and call for further investigation of more aggressive treatment in men.
critique: The number of treated metastases is irreconcilable within the paper. The abstract and Table 1 give 384 lesions, the results text says 452, and Table 1's mean of 6 plus or minus 0.5 lesions across 63 patients implies about 378. The per-lesion local recurrence rate of 6.3% depends on which denominator is used.

The entire univariate predictor table is built on 62 patients, not 63, and the sex split changes between tables: Table 1 and the results give 41 men and 22 women, Table 6 gives 41 and 21. Extrahepatic disease is present in 24 patients (38.1%) in the text and Table 3 but in 21 patients in Table 6, and the chromogranin A rows sum to only 41 patients.

The multivariable Cox model carries four covariates on 25 deaths, with candidates admitted on a univariate screen at P<.10, and both significant hazard ratios have confidence intervals that barely clear 1 (1.1 to 9.1 and 1.1 to 10.1). Table 7's two liver-volume rows carry hazard ratios of 0.9 and 1.8 with identical upper confidence bounds of 2.8, which cannot both be right.

The dominant-tumour-size effect weakens sharply when the survival clock is moved earlier: P=.005 measured from ablation but P=.05 measured from diagnosis of liver metastases. That pattern is what referral timing rather than biology would produce.

This cohort is a subset of the same group's later 89-patient series, and the two papers reach opposite conclusions on the strongest variable: extrahepatic disease has no effect here (P=.85) and is the most significant predictor there (P=.0001, median 26 versus 133 months).

A core-needle biopsy of a representative lesion was taken under ultrasound in every patient to confirm histology, and no grade, Ki-67, mitotic rate or differentiation is reported anywhere. Tissue was in hand and the variable that now governs management of these patients was not measured.

The study is described as a phase II protocol, yet no prespecified primary endpoint, sample size calculation or protocol-defined response criteria appear. The methods promise objective tumour response on serial triphasic CT and no objective response rate is ever reported.

The 80% liver-progression figure is calculated on the 45 patients with at least 3 months of imaging, excluding 18 of 63. The patients excluded are those who were lost or died earliest, which is the group whose disease was progressing fastest.

The median duration of symptom control is calculated on the 33 responders only, dropping the 2 non-responders, and is reported as a median plus or minus a standard error of the mean. Symptom response itself was graded at one week as complete, significant, moderate or minimal by unblinded surgeon assessment, with no definitions and no instrument.

The finding that repeat ablation did not reduce survival is confounded by design. The methods state that patients with numerous, diffuse and rapidly progressing lesions were recommended for alternative therapy, so the worst progressors were channelled out of the repeat-ablation group before the comparison was made.

Table 6's progression stratum compares progression within 6 months against progression after 12 months, omitting entirely the patients who progressed between 6 and 12 months, and concludes that timing of progression does not affect survival.

Survival is reported from three different time zeros (11.0, 5.5 and 3.9 years) against a mean follow-up of only 2.8 plus or minus 0.3 years, so the 5-year rates and the unreached medians for women and for lesions under 3 cm are extrapolations beyond the observed data.
The 48% five-year survival after ablation is set against a cited 61% after resection and discussed as underscoring the place of RFA; the comparison runs the wrong way and the paper does not say so.

The cohort includes 9 medullary thyroid cancers, 4 bronchial carcinoids and 1 undifferentiated neuroendocrine tumour, so almost a quarter of the series lies outside the gastroenteropancreatic population to which the conclusions are applied.

The ablation catheter is a named commercial device (RITA Medical Systems) and two of the cited supporting references are the same authors' own clinical evaluations of that manufacturer's catheter. The paper carries no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration.
A search of PubMed found no linked editorial or comment for this paper, and unlike the authors' 2010 series no podium discussion is printed with it, so no external appraisal is available.
17629995.n: 63 patients with 384 neuroendocrine liver metastases treated in 80 laparoscopic ablation sessions, selected from 524 patients with 1636 primary and secondary liver tumours ablated by one surgeon between January 1996 and October 2005.
17629995.bottom_line: This shows that laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation can be delivered to unresectable, liver-dominant neuroendocrine metastases with 5% morbidity, no deaths, a 1.1-day stay and symptom relief in 94% of symptomatic patients lasting a median of 11 months. It does not show that ablation changes the course of the disease: 80% of imaged patients developed new or progressive liver disease, the survival figures are quoted from three different starting points against a mean follow-up of 2.8 years, and the two independent predictors rest on a four-covariate model with 25 deaths and confidence intervals that barely exclude 1. Tissue was biopsied in every patient and grade was never reported, so the series cannot be read onto the G1/G2 distinctions that now decide who is offered ablation.

limitations: As a retrospective review from multiple centres the data are incomplete, and the authors state they are continuing the collaboration to capture the proportion of patients symptomatic before and after treatment, the duration of symptomatic and radiographic response, and tumour marker response.

Imaging technique was not standardised and a single response system was not applied; where WHO or RECIST criteria could not be used because the pre- and post-treatment imaging differed, a best estimate of response was given.
The authors name standardising the imaging technique, the response system and the interval between scans in the first 6 months as work still to be done.
No quality-of-life measures were collected; the authors note that EORTC global and liver-specific tools should be included in future analyses of radioembolisation.
Participation was voluntary and, the project being unfunded, the response to join was modest; institutions in Australia and Asia were not approached at all, for want of established relationships.
Specific data could not be found for some patients, so every result is reported as the number with data available over the total possible.
The partition method of activity calculation cannot be applied in neuroendocrine metastases because it requires a single well-defined tumour, so body surface area dosimetry was used throughout.
critique: The response percentages are computed over a denominator that includes the treatments that could not be assessed. Only 168 of 185 treatments were assessable, yet partial response is given as 112/185 (60.5%), complete response 5/185, stable disease 42/185 and progression 9/185, so the four categories sum to 90.8% and the 17 unassessable treatments silently dilute every rate.

Response is reported per treatment rather than per patient, so the 22.3% of patients retreated and the centres that deliberately treat one lobe then the other contribute two or three response observations each to a denominator of 185 treatments in 148 people.

The toxicity accounting does not close either. Grade 3 to 4 data were available for 161 of 185 treatments, the rates are nonetheless given over 185, and the statement that no grade 3 to 4 toxicity occurred in 124 of 185 treatments leaves 61 treatments unaccounted for by the handful of listed events.

The median survival of 70 months is reported with 77.7% of patients still alive and a median follow-up of 42 months. The estimate therefore comes from the far tail of a heavily censored curve, and no confidence interval and no numbers at risk are given anywhere.

Survival is timed from the first microsphere treatment in a cohort that, by the stated inclusion criterion, had already completed comprehensive evaluation and treatment of the primary tumour and its metastases. These are survivors of earlier therapy, and prior treatment is nowhere quantified, so the line of therapy this 70-month figure represents is unknown.

The methods define a four-level tumour marker response scale using chromogranin A, serotonin and occasionally 24-hour 5-HIAA, and no marker result appears anywhere in the paper. The discussion lists marker response among the things the collaboration still intends to collect.

The lung shunt exclusion was breached without separate analysis. The stated threshold was 20% and patients were treated with shunt fractions up to 34.1%; how many, and what happened to them, is not reported.

Delivered activity ranged from 38.1% to 147.4% of the body-surface-area prescription, and that percentage was recorded for only 132 of 185 procedures. A delivery of nearly one and a half times the prescribed activity is neither flagged as a deviation nor related to the toxicity data, and the reasons for reduced delivery were not captured.

The safety claim rests on a dosimetry method chosen precisely so that dose need not be measured. Body surface area prescribing is a manufacturer-suggested convention and the paper reports no absorbed dose to tumour or to uninvolved liver, so 'no radiation-induced liver disease' is a statement about clinical observation with no dose denominator behind it.

Radiation-induced liver injury in this disease is a late effect and this cohort is young in follow-up terms, with 78% alive at a median of 42 months. The same question asked later with longer follow-up found progressive alkaline phosphatase and transaminase elevation and imaging features of portal hypertension after sequential lobar treatment, which this series would not have been positioned to see.

Thirty-three patients had the same liver volume treated two or three times and no cumulative-activity or cumulative-dose analysis is presented, even though repeated irradiation of the same parenchyma is the main theoretical route to late liver injury.

Data were abstracted locally at ten voluntarily participating centres with no central imaging review, no source-data verification and no audit, and every participating team is characterised in the paper as a centre of excellence for radioembolisation. The response and toxicity figures therefore describe best-case expert practice at self-selected sites.

Tables 5 to 8 set the series' own figures beside collected surgical, chemoembolisation, radiopeptide and 131I-MIBG series from the literature without any formal comparison, matching or adjustment, and the discussion draws its favourable reading from those side-by-side tables.

Neither grade nor Ki-67 is reported, 82% of the cohort is recorded only as carcinoid, and the one patient who developed ascites is noted to have had concurrent hepatic progression, so even that single event is attributed away without analysis.

The product studied is a single manufacturer's resin microsphere and the dosimetry follows that manufacturer's recommendation, and the paper carries no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration of any kind; the authors describe the project only as unfunded. A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
18525307.n: 148 patients with unresectable neuroendocrine liver metastases treated with resin yttrium-90 microspheres in 185 procedures at 10 North American and European centres, all described as centres of excellence for radioembolisation, with most patients and treatments contributed by half of them; median follow-up 42 months.
18525307.bottom_line: This is the first multicentre series of resin yttrium-90 radioembolisation dedicated to neuroendocrine liver metastases, and what it establishes is tolerability: across 185 procedures in 148 patients, grade 3 to 4 events were uncommon, no radiation-induced liver disease occurred and retreatment of the same volume in 22% caused no liver failure. The efficacy figures should not be carried further than that: a 63% objective response is scored per treatment on non-standardised imaging with a best-estimate category where RECIST could not be applied, the percentages are computed over a denominator that includes unassessable treatments, and the 70-month median survival comes from a curve on which 78% of patients were still alive at a median follow-up of 42 months. With no comparator, no quality-of-life data, no tumour-marker results despite a defined scale for them, and no grade or Ki-67, it cannot say what radioembolisation adds or to whom.
18525307.funding: The authors describe the project as unfunded, which is why participation was limited; no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration appears anywhere in the paper.

limitations: Treatment after progression was at the discretion of each centre; most placebo patients went on to a somatostatin analogue and many on the active arm continued it, so long-term observation of patients not receiving octreotide LAR is difficult and no conclusion about overall survival can be drawn from this trial.

The protocol specified that the analysis of time to tumour-related death be based on 121 events; because of the observed effect on tumour growth and a slow recruitment rate the authors stopped further enrolment, without unblinding the nine patients still on treatment.
The number of patients with high hepatic tumour burden was low, and the authors state that the role of hepatic tumour load needs investigating in more depth.
Whether the favourable effect on time to tumour progression translates into prolonged overall survival, an important secondary aim, could not be determined.
Whether patients with a high hepatic tumour burden that developed slowly respond more favourably to biotherapy requires further study.
The result applies to midgut primaries only; the authors call for studies in neuroendocrine tumours of other origins.
critique: The effect size comes from an interim analysis at a prespecified local alpha of 0.0122, after which recruitment was stopped because the result was positive. A trial halted early on an efficacy boundary systematically overstates the treatment effect, and PROMID enrolled 85 of a planned 162 patients, so its hazard ratio of 0.32 to 0.34 is the most favourable point in the trial's history rather than its final estimate.

Three different hazard ratios are available for the same comparison (conservative intent-to-treat 0.34, planned intent-to-treat 0.32, per-protocol 0.24), and the subgroup analyses most often quoted in clinical discussion come from the per-protocol set, the most selected of the three.

The subgroup results that drive practice cannot exclude no effect. The hazard ratio of 0.17 at 0 to 10% liver involvement comes from strata of roughly 7 to 14 patients, while the intervals at 10 to 50% (0.10 to 1.67) and above 50% (0.11 to 4.45) include both large benefit and substantial harm, and no interaction test is reported. The claim that octreotide LAR is the treatment of choice in low hepatic load rests on a comparison the trial was never powered to make.

Resection of the primary (HR 0.16 against 0.84 unresected) is similarly exploratory and is confounded with disease extent, since patients whose primary was resectable are not the same patients as those whose was not.

Progression was read by bidimensional WHO criteria, which register a given amount of growth as a larger percentage change than unidimensional RECIST. CLARINET's authors made precisely this point about PROMID, and it is one reason the 6.0-month placebo median here sits so far from CLARINET's 18.0 months.

The primary endpoint is time to tumour progression, not progression-free survival, so deaths without documented progression are censored rather than counted as events. In a disease whose patients die of liver failure, that choice is not neutral.

Nothing in the symptom or quality-of-life data supports the drug. No difference reached significance in the EORTC QLQ-C30 scores, symptomatic response or biochemical response tables, with p values as high as .1106, in a trial that includes functioning tumours and a drug whose original indication is symptom control.

The population is close to the most indolent that exists: 95% had a Ki-67 of 2% or less, 61% had 10% or less liver involvement, 66% had the primary resected, and all were treatment-naive with no curative option. Grade 2 midgut disease and any pancreatic primary are outside the evidence entirely.

With 16 deaths the survival comparison carries no information (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.18), and the placebo median of 73.7 months is longer than the trial could observe, so the figure most often used to characterise untreated midgut NET comes from an immature curve.

The conclusion extends the result to a population the trial never contained: the authors propose octreotide LAR as an attractive option after cytoreductive surgery with few remaining metastases, when PROMID excluded patients with any curative option and performed no liver surgery as part of the study.

Five of the six gallstone events occurred on octreotide and five patients stopped the drug for adverse events against none on placebo, in a population who may subsequently require hepatectomy or hepatic arterial therapy. The safety paragraph records similar serious-adverse-event counts and no treatment-related deaths without drawing that implication.

The trial ran at 18 academic centres in a single country over seven years, averaging under one patient per centre per year, and ended with 9 patients still blinded and on treatment, so the dataset is incomplete by design and cannot be completed.

Novartis, which markets octreotide LAR, funded the trial, supplied the drug and participated in developing the study design, and the disclosure block lists Novartis honoraria for three authors and Novartis research funding for four. The paper states the company took no part in data collection, analysis or interpretation.

A linked editorial accompanies the trial in the same issue (Oberg, 'Is it time to widen the use of somatostatin analogs in neuroendocrine tumors?', J Clin Oncol 2009;27:4635-6, PMID 19704053). Its full text was not obtained, so none of the points above draws on it.
19704057.n: 85 treatment-naive patients with well-differentiated, locally inoperable or metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumours randomised 1:1 at 18 German academic centres between March 2001 and January 2008, out of 90 enrolled and against a planned sample of 162; reported at the planned interim analysis after 67 progressions and 16 deaths, with 9 patients still on treatment and never unblinded.
19704057.bottom_line: PROMID is the trial that converted somatostatin analogues from symptom control into antitumour therapy, showing a median time to tumour progression of 14.3 against 6.0 months with a hazard ratio of about 0.33 in treatment-naive metastatic midgut NET. Its effect is stabilisation, not shrinkage (one partial response in each arm), and it establishes nothing about survival, symptoms or quality of life: only 16 deaths had occurred, the placebo arm went on to somatostatin analogues after progression, and no symptom or quality-of-life comparison reached significance. The benefit is concentrated where the disease is least threatening, with hazard ratios of 0.17, 0.40 and 0.71 across 0-10%, 10-50% and over 50% hepatic involvement on strata of a dozen patients, so the trial's own data argue that a patient with a heavy liver burden is the one it speaks least to.
19704057.funding: Supported by grants from Novartis, Nuremberg, Germany, which participated in developing the study design and provided the active medication and the funding but, per the paper, took no part in data collection, analysis or interpretation. Declared interests: Novartis honoraria to A. Rinke, M. Blaker and R. Arnold; Novartis research funding to A. Rinke, K.-J. Klose, P. Barth and R. Arnold.

limitations: The paper carries no limitations section; the concessions below are scattered through the introduction, discussion and the printed podium discussion.
Given the complex and select group of patients in this series, the authors state it is not possible to compare RFA directly with other treatment modalities.

Despite 92% local tumour control, new liver and extrahepatic recurrence occurred in about 60% of patients, which the authors read as showing that systemic control of the disease is necessary for overall prognosis.
Liver-directed surgery should be regarded as a debulking operation, as many of these patients have a high rate of recurrence.
The female survival advantage the same group had previously reported held on univariate analysis but disappeared on multivariate analysis.
Asked from the floor whether pathological differentiation, Ki-67 and mitotic rate had been examined, the senior author answered that this analysis was not done.
The authors concede that hepatectomy still has a role in patients with bulky resectable disease too large for ablation.
critique: The survival analysis loses ten patients without explanation. The results text reports 54 men and 35 women, but Table I's gender rows list 54 male and 25 female, which sums to 79 rather than 89; the other Table I strata (tumour type, number of metastases, liver tumour volume, extrahepatic disease) each sum to 89.

Table II gives hazard ratios with no confidence intervals at all, so the precision of the three independent predictors cannot be judged; liver tumour volume is entered as a single variable with one P value (.047 in the text, .04 in the table) covering two hazard ratios of 1.2 and 3.5.

The methods state that objective tumour response was assessed on triphasic CT one week before and one week after ablation, and no response rate of any kind appears in the results. The only efficacy numbers reported are survival, symptoms and recurrence.

Local control is quoted two ways and the conclusion uses the flattering one. Local recurrence was 22% per patient but 7.9% per lesion, and the discussion converts the per-lesion figure into '92% local tumor control' against a denominator of 547 lesions.

The 57% five-year survival is set beside historical figures of 61% after resection, 36% after transplantation and 42% after chemotherapy (references 21 to 23) and described as comparing favourably, when it is in fact lower than the resection figure and the series entered patients at a different point in their disease.
Median follow-up was 30 plus or minus 3 months against a median survival of 6 years, so the whole tail of the Kaplan-Meier curve rests on few patients; no figure in the paper reports numbers at risk.

The survival clock starts at the first ablation, and the median interval from diagnosis of liver metastases to RFA was 10 months (range 1 to 108). Patients had to survive to referral to enter the cohort, which inflates survival measured from that point.

Patients with synchronous metastases had a median survival of 133 months versus 33 months for metachronous (P=.08), the opposite of the expected direction. The paper reports the figure and offers no explanation, which is the signal one would expect if the metachronous group was referred later in its disease course.

Outcomes cannot be attributed to the index ablation. During follow-up octreotide was given in 30%, repeat RFA in 27%, chemotherapy in 18% and chemoembolisation in 10%, and patients with multifocal recurrence were deliberately moved to chemoembolisation.

The recommendation that patients 'might need to be referred earlier to improve their survival' rests only on liver tumour volume being prognostic in a cross-sectional cohort. No comparison of earlier versus later ablation was performed, so prognostic value is being read as benefit from earlier intervention.

The cohort is not the gastroenteropancreatic G1/G2 population of current pathways: 11 of 89 primaries were medullary thyroid cancer and 6 were bronchial carcinoid, and tumour type was declared non-significant (P=.2) on 11 medullary and 23 islet-cell patients with the medullary median not reached.

Chromogranin A was analysed in only 61 of 89 patients (41 at 39 to 150 U/L and 20 above 150 in Table I), so the marker with the clearest link to hormonal symptoms is missing for a third of the cohort.

Everything continuous is reported as mean plus or minus standard error of the mean rather than standard deviation, which makes the spread look far tighter than it is (tumour size 3.6 plus or minus 0.2 cm for a range of 1 to 10 cm), and the median symptom duration is given as 14 plus or minus 5 months, mixing a median with a standard error.
Internal figures disagree between the abstract and the results: morbidity 6% versus 5.6%, and median disease-free survival 1.3 years versus 15 months.
A named radiofrequency catheter and generator setting are discussed in detail at the podium, and the paper contains no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration of any kind.
A search of PubMed found no linked editorial or comment for this paper; the only external commentary available is the discussion printed with the article itself.
21134563.n: 89 patients with 547 neuroendocrine liver metastases who underwent 119 laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation sessions at one centre between January 1996 and August 2009; 64 had a single session, 19 had two, 4 had three and 1 had four.
21134563.bottom_line: This establishes that laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation of neuroendocrine liver metastases is safe and durably palliative in experienced hands, with 5.6% morbidity, a 1.1-day stay, 97% at least partial symptom relief and 92% per-lesion local control in the largest series assembled. It establishes nothing about survival benefit: the 6-year median and 57% five-year figures come from a single arm selected for under 20% liver volume, at most 15 lesions and liver-dominant disease, timed from the ablation rather than from diagnosis, with octreotide, repeat ablation, chemotherapy and embolisation layered on afterwards. Because differentiation and Ki-67 were never examined, the cohort cannot be mapped onto the grade distinctions that now determine which of these patients should be ablated at all.

limitations: The paper has no limitations section; the concessions below are made within the discussion.
The authors acknowledge that early termination of clinical trials may result in overestimation of the true treatment effect and in lower-than-anticipated numbers of enrolled patients.

The trial was terminated early because of the risk of serious adverse events, disease progression and death among patients receiving placebo, that is on the strength of harm in the control arm rather than only on efficacy.
The blinded independent central review that supports the investigator-assessed primary endpoint was retrospective and covered only 49% of patients (84 of 171).
The exploratory subgroup analysis contained small numbers of patients in some subgroups.
Numerical between-group differences in some baseline characteristics were present, which the authors address with post hoc testing rather than adjustment.
Most sunitinib-related adverse events required dose interruption or modification to manage.
critique: The headline result did not formally cross the trial's own threshold. The observed test statistic for progression-free survival was z = 3.85 against a prespecified Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming boundary of 3.88, and the trial was stopped anyway. The reported P value of less than 0.001 should be read against that boundary, not against 0.05.
The trial was halted at half its planned size, 171 of 340 patients and 81 of 260 events, so the effect estimate is both the maximum observed and the least precise the protocol contemplated.

Censoring runs in opposite directions in the two arms. Progression-free survival data were censored in 65% of sunitinib patients against 40% on placebo, and 48% of sunitinib patients left the trial because it was terminated against 19% on placebo. Differential censoring of this size is not neutral with respect to the curve that produced the hazard ratio.

The reassurance about baseline imbalance is explicitly unreported. The paper states that univariate and multivariate analysis showed the imbalanced factors had no effect on the progression-free survival benefit, followed by 'data not shown'.

Baseline differences in a randomised trial are handled by adjustment, not by hypothesis testing, and the paper uses post hoc Fisher's exact tests to conclude there were no significant differences in baseline factors. A non-significant p value on a baseline table says nothing about confounding in a 171-patient trial.

The primary endpoint was assessed by unblinded investigators using RECIST, with central review applied retrospectively to half the cohort, in a trial that was unblinded at closure and whose placebo patients were then offered open-label sunitinib.

The survival claim in the final sentence rests on 30 deaths with medians not reached in either arm and 59 of 82 placebo patients crossing over to open-label sunitinib. A hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% CI 0.19-0.89) from that configuration cannot support the stated clinically meaningful improvement in overall survival.

The quality-of-life claim is imported from elsewhere. The discussion cites a recently reported post hoc analysis for a delay in time to deterioration, while this paper's own quality-of-life data show a clinically and statistically significant worsening of diarrhoea by 21.4 points and no difference in global health status.

The observation that other serious adverse events were less common on sunitinib than placebo (26% against 41%) reflects unchecked disease progression in the control arm, and that same observation was part of the justification for stopping the trial. It is not a safety advantage of the drug.

A 9.3% response rate with 2 complete and 6 partial responses in 83 patients means the drug stabilises rather than shrinks disease, so nothing here supports sunitinib as a way of converting unresectable hepatic disease to resectable.

Grading was largely unmeasured. Ki-67 was evaluable in only about 36 of 86 and 36 of 85 patients, the subgroup with Ki-67 above 5% (n = 29) showed only a trend, and no somatostatin receptor imaging was required, so the population cannot be mapped onto current grade-based or receptor-based pathways.

Somatostatin analogues were permitted at investigator discretion and used in 68 patients, without stratification, in a trial run just before PROMID and CLARINET made them standard. The control arm therefore received an uncontrolled amount of an agent now known to delay progression.

Tolerability is understated by presentation. Dose reduction to 25 mg was needed in 31% and interruption in 30%, grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 12% and hypertension in 10%, discontinuation for adverse events doubled, and one patient died of treatment-related cardiac failure, all for a median gain of 5.9 months in radiographic progression.

Ninety-five per cent of patients had distant metastases, mostly hepatic, and the paper reports no hepatic tumour burden, no liver-specific endpoint and no information about prior or subsequent liver-directed therapy, so it cannot be used to position sunitinib relative to embolisation or resection.

The sponsor ran the trial. Pfizer designed it in conjunction with the investigators, collected the data, performed the statistical analyses and paid the professional medical writers who helped prepare the first draft, and two co-authors are Pfizer Oncology employees.
Three correspondence items are linked to this paper in PubMed (PMIDs 21561356, 21561357, 21561358). None of their full texts was obtained, so whatever objections they raise are not represented here.
21306237.n: 171 patients with well-differentiated, advanced or metastatic, inoperable pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours progressing within the previous 12 months, randomised 1:1 at 42 centres in 11 countries between June 2007 and April 2009 against a planned enrolment of 340; the trial closed early at 81 of a planned 260 progression events, with 83 and 82 patients in the safety population.
21306237.bottom_line: This trial established sunitinib 37.5 mg daily as a treatment for progressive, well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, roughly doubling median progression-free survival from 5.5 to 11.4 months with a hazard ratio of 0.42. The result is weaker than its reputation: the trial was stopped at half its planned size with a test statistic (z=3.85) that did not reach its own efficacy boundary (3.88), progression was judged by unblinded investigators with retrospective central review in only half the patients, and censoring was 65% against 40% between the arms. The response rate was 9.3%, the survival claim rests on 30 deaths with most of the placebo arm crossing over, and the only quality-of-life signal in the paper itself is worse diarrhoea, so this is a drug for delaying progression and not for converting hepatic disease.
21306237.funding: Supported by Pfizer, which designed the trial in conjunction with the investigators, collected the data, performed the statistical analyses and paid the professional medical writers who collaborated on the first draft; two co-authors are Pfizer Oncology employees. Declared interests include board membership, grant support and payment for educational presentations from Pfizer and Novartis for the first author, and consulting or travel fees from Pfizer for several co-authors.

limitations: The paper has no limitations section; the concessions below appear in the results and discussion.
The authors state that patients assigned to placebo could switch to open-label everolimus on progression, which confounds the detection of a treatment-related survival benefit.
Exposure to study drug was far longer in the everolimus arm, which the authors note when comparing adverse-event rates with other trials.

Non-infectious pneumonitis and interstitial lung disease, recognised class effects of rapamycin derivatives, were observed, and the authors state only that they can be managed according to existing guidelines.
Atypical infections including pulmonary tuberculosis, bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and reactivation of hepatitis B each occurred in one patient in association with everolimus.
Whether everolimus and sunitinib can be combined, and whether that would increase antitumour activity, is explicitly left unresolved.
The molecular pathogenesis of sporadic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours is unknown, so the mTOR rationale rests on indirect evidence from genetic syndromes and from paired-biopsy proliferation data.
critique: The trial can never answer the survival question, by design. Seventy-three per cent of the placebo arm crossed over to open-label everolimus, the observed hazard ratio for death is 1.05 (95% CI 0.71-1.55), and no amount of further follow-up will recover an interpretable comparison.

The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed, in a trial whose entry criterion was progression judged locally as an unequivocal increase in tumour size within 12 months. Central adjudicated review agreed closely, which is reassuring, but it was a supportive analysis rather than the registrational endpoint.

Five per cent of patients had a confirmed partial response and none had a complete response. The drug prevents measurable growth; it does not shrink tumours, so it cannot be used to convert unresectable hepatic disease.

Censoring was markedly asymmetric, with progression-free survival data censored in 47% of the everolimus arm against 19% of the placebo arm, while exposure differed by a factor of 2.3 (38 against 16 weeks). The first flatters the progression-free survival curve and the second understates everolimus toxicity per unit of time at risk.

The control arm is placebo with best supportive care in which a somatostatin analogue was given to only about 40% of patients. The trial ran in parallel with PROMID and predates CLARINET, so by any current standard the comparator is undertreated.

There is no comparison with any active agent: not streptozocin-based chemotherapy, which was the established cytotoxic option at the time, and not capecitabine-temozolomide or PRRT, which have since become the real competitors. The trial establishes activity, not position in a sequence.

Patients embolised within 6 months, or ablated or cryoablated within 2 months, were excluded, and over 90% of the cohort had liver metastases. The trial therefore says nothing about everolimus in patients who have had or are being considered for liver-directed therapy, and reports no hepatic tumour burden at all.

Toxicity is presented as mild because most events were grade 1 or 2, while 13% of patients discontinued for drug-related adverse events against 2% on placebo, dose adjustment was needed for stomatitis in 10%, pneumonitis in 7% and thrombocytopenia in 7%, and one patient died of treatment-related acute respiratory distress syndrome.

The pneumonitis signal is reported in pieces. Pneumonitis occurred in 12% and interstitial lung disease in 2% against 0% on placebo, glucocorticoids were given to six of the seven patients with grade 3 or 4 events, and the discussion records that only 5 of those events (2%) were considered drug-related, which reclassifies most of the severe cases away from the drug.
Twenty-four per cent of patients had a functioning tumour and no hormonal symptom outcome is reported, nor any quality-of-life result, in a disease where symptom control is often the reason to treat.
Grade was determined locally by low or intermediate category rather than by central Ki-67, so the grade subgroup consistency the paper reports is consistency across locally assigned labels.

The sponsor built and analysed the trial: Novartis Oncology co-designed it with the academic investigators, the data were collected on the sponsor's data management systems and analysed by the sponsor's statistical team, and the first draft was written by the first author together with a Novartis Oncology medical writer, with further manuscript assistance from a communications agency.

A linked editorial (Jensen and Delle Fave, N Engl J Med 2011;364:564-565, PMID 21306243) and correspondence covering this trial and the companion sunitinib trial (PMID 21561355 and the letters at NEJMc1102746) accompany the paper. None of those texts was obtained, so no position is attributed to them here.
21306238.n: 410 patients with advanced low- or intermediate-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and radiologic progression within the previous 12 months, randomised at 82 centres in 18 countries between July 2007 and May 2009: 207 to everolimus 10 mg daily and 203 to placebo; over 90% had liver metastases, 24% a functioning tumour, and 148 of the 203 placebo patients (73%) later crossed over to open-label everolimus.
21306238.bottom_line: RADIANT-3 established everolimus 10 mg daily as a treatment for progressive advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, more than doubling median progression-free survival from 4.6 to 11.0 months (hazard ratio 0.35), with blinded central review in close agreement. The benefit is stabilisation and nothing more: 5% had a partial response, none a complete one, and because 73% of the placebo arm crossed over the trial can never show whether everolimus lets anyone live longer, with the observed hazard ratio for death at 1.05. Patients embolised within 6 months or ablated within 2 months were excluded and no hepatic tumour burden is reported, so in a cohort over 90% liver-metastatic the trial offers no guidance on sequencing everolimus with liver-directed treatment.
21306238.funding: Supported by Novartis Oncology. The study was designed by the academic investigators together with representatives of the sponsor; the data were collected using the sponsor's data management systems and analysed by the sponsor's statistical team; the first draft was prepared by the first author with a medical writer employed by Novartis Oncology, with further manuscript assistance acknowledged from ApotheCom. One co-author is affiliated to Novartis Oncology.

limitations: The high incidence of bilomas was unexpected and forced interruption of the trial.
The resulting changes in technique and patient selection are based on a small number of patients and the authors call them speculative.
The cause of biloma formation was likely multifactorial, with patient factors (number and size of tumours) and procedural factors (drug delivery technique) both implicated.

The beads were mixed with contrast 1:1 and could not be seen when injected into the hepatic artery; the embolisation endpoint was judged from the operator's tactile response, which the authors say may have led to overembolisation and bead deposition outside the tumour.
Because these patients had more widespread disease and liver involvement, selective placement of the microcatheter was often not feasible.
The authors concede their 54% biloma rate is much greater than the 9.6% reported after conventional TACE for metastatic liver tumours, although in a population of only 13.

They accept that the smaller bead size used here (100 to 300 micron) against the 500 to 700 micron particles of the de Baere series could itself be a predisposing factor by causing more profound ischaemic change in the peribiliary plexus.

One patient with a pre-existing biliary-enteric anastomosis was treated despite the known increase in abscess risk, on the authors' judgement that benefit would outweigh risk; that patient developed a biloma and died.
Chemoembolisation has not shown a survival benefit in randomised controlled trials, a point the authors make in the introduction.
critique: The abstract's account of who was harmed contradicts the paper's own table. The abstract states that all seven patients who developed bilomas had multiple small lesions under 4 cm, while Table 3 classes two of the seven as single lesions with or without satellites and two as multiple lesions whose smallest was 3.5 cm, and the discussion says only two of the seven had multiple lesions. The recommendation that follows, to treat only patients whose smallest lesion exceeds 4 cm, is built on the abstract's version.

The reported biloma volume silently excludes the largest biloma. The text gives 32.4 plus or minus 35.3 cm3 with a range of 1.7 to 83.2 cm3 and refers the reader to Table 3, which lists a volume of 394.42 cm3 in patient 3, the patient drained for mass effect. The 7.3 cm3 drainage threshold is then derived from the same seven observations.

Two patients died of treatment-related sepsis after biloma and abscess, and the results section states there were no deaths within 30 days of treatment and that, aside from the bilomas, the toxicity profile was limited and predominantly lower grade. The paper never reports when those two deaths occurred or gives a 90-day mortality.

The CTCAE table understates the event that stopped the trial. Biloma appears as a grade 3 to 4 toxicity in 8% (1 patient) and liver abscess in 15% (1 patient, labelled as 15% for a single patient of 13), while the narrative reports bilomas in 54% and drainage in 31%.

The protocol change rests on a non-significant difference. Biloma patients had a mean hepatic tumour burden of 12% against 44% in those without, at P=0.06, and the subgroup text gives those same figures as 14% versus 45% with the p value printed as 'n = 0.06'. On that basis small multifocal disease was removed from eligibility.

The headline 78% response is the most favourable of four figures the paper could have quoted. By RECIST there were no complete and only 16% partial responses per lesion at 1 month, and 0% objective response per patient (all 13 stable); EASL per patient gives 62%. The abstract reports the per-lesion EASL figure.
Per-lesion statistics treat 32 lesions in 13 patients as independent observations, with paired tests and p values down to P<0.0001, and no adjustment for clustering within patients.

The efficacy denominators collapse with time and the paper does not say why. Thirty-two lesions in 13 patients at 1 month become 26 lesions in 10 patients at 6 months and 19 lesions in 6 patients at 12 months, so the 53% twelve-month response rate describes fewer than half the enrolled patients, in a trial where two died of complications and enrolment was halted.

Mean tumour size is larger at 12 months (3.4 cm) than at 6 months (3.1 cm) while the reported change from baseline grows from minus 30% to minus 40%, because each time point is a different subset of lesions. The table presents the series as a single declining trajectory.

Tables 6 and 7 carry the identical caption 'Efficacy: response by RECIST/EASL criteria per lesion' although Table 7 is a per-patient analysis, so the two response denominators that matter most are labelled the same way.

No survival, progression-free survival or time-to-progression is reported at any point, and the only symptom outcome is the unmeasured statement that all three patients with carcinoid syndrome had remission; no symptom instrument was used.

Enhancement on contrast MRI, measured by a semiautomatic three-dimensional segmentation tool, carries the efficacy claim. Enhancement necessarily falls after arterial embolisation whether or not tumour is killed, no central or blinded read is described, and a co-author is affiliated to Philips Research North America, whose clinical informatics group develops such quantification software.

The trial was partially funded by Biocompatibles UK Ltd, which manufactures the LC Bead product under test, and the senior author declares that funding. The abstract concludes that the technique was efficacious and that the trial could resume after the authors changed their own technique and selection criteria.

The comparison that makes the 54% rate interpretable is left to the reader to assemble. The paper itself cites 9.6% biloma after conventional TACE for liver metastases, about 30% biliary injury with none requiring drainage in the Guiu series, and 0% in de Baere's drug-eluting bead series using 500 to 700 micron particles, but runs no formal comparison and has no internal control arm.
Mean age is 64 in Table 1 and 65 in the abstract, and the discussion states that 92% had stable disease at 1 month, a figure that matches neither Table 6 nor Table 7.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so the biliary-injury signal reached the literature without independent appraisal until the RETNET trial closed its drug-eluting bead arm.
22722717.n: 13 patients with histologically confirmed unresectable neuroendocrine liver metastases enrolled from May 2009 through August 2010, treated in 27 DEB-TACE procedures (median 2 per patient, range 1 to 4), reported as the interim safety analysis that forced interruption of the trial.
22722717.bottom_line: This is the paper that put a number on biliary injury after drug-eluting bead chemoembolisation of neuroendocrine liver metastases: 7 bilomas in 13 patients (54%), four drained, two deaths after prolonged infection, enough to halt a phase II trial and to change the centre's technique and selection criteria. It establishes almost nothing about efficacy, because the 78% figure is EASL enhancement response counted per targeted lesion at one month, RECIST per-patient objective response was zero, and no survival or progression endpoint is reported at all. The mechanism it proposes, that small-volume multifocal disease predisposes to injury, rests on a non-significant comparison (12% versus 44% burden, P=0.06) and on an abstract claim about lesion size that the paper's own table contradicts.
22722717.funding: Partially funded by National Institutes of Health Grant R01 CA160771-2 and by BioCompatibles UK Ltd, the manufacturer of the drug-eluting bead under study. N. Bhagat, M. Lin and J.-F. Geschwind were partially funded by the NIH grant; J.-F. Geschwind was partially funded by Biocompatibles UK Ltd.

limitations: 96% of patients had stable disease at baseline, and such patients are likely to have fewer tumour-related events than patients with progressive disease.
Data are lacking from controlled trials in patients with documented progressive disease.

No significant between-group difference in overall survival was apparent at 2 years, which the authors attribute to the long life expectancy of slow-growing tumours and to crossover from placebo to active treatment at progression.
Only patients with non-functioning tumours were enrolled, whereas PROMID included some mildly functioning tumours.
The durability of the antiproliferative effect remains to be determined and is being examined in the CLARINET extension study.

The comparison with PROMID's shorter placebo-arm time to progression cannot be resolved, because progression status was not documented in PROMID and the two trials used different criteria, bidimensional WHO against unidimensional RECIST 1.0, which alone could shorten apparent progression-free survival.
The authors accept that individualised treatment remains the cornerstone of management and that deferred treatment will continue to be appropriate for some patients.
They acknowledge that their placebo group can be read as a surrogate for deferred treatment and that its long progression-free survival may appear to support a wait-and-see policy.
critique: The subgroup that matters most for liver-directed decisions is a post hoc construction. Hepatic tumour volume was prespecified in five categories whose estimated hazard ratios ranged from 0.24 to 0.54, and was collapsed after the fact into a dichotomy at 25%. The conclusion that the effect holds irrespective of hepatic tumour volume rests on that simplification, as the paper's own table footnote states.

Benefit in grade 2 disease is not demonstrated. The grade 2 hazard ratio is 0.58 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.32 to 1.04, which includes 1, while the trial's headline and its licensed indication cover grade 1 and grade 2 together.

Every subgroup estimate rests on a handful of events. The trial recorded 92 progression events in all, so the midgut (0.35), pancreas (0.45) and high-hepatic-volume (0.45, CI 0.22 to 0.91) hazard ratios each come from fewer than 30 events, and no interaction test is reported for any of them.

The whole benefit is radiographic. Overall survival did not differ, EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status did not differ, and the population was non-functioning by design so there were no hormonal symptoms to improve. Crossover is invoked to explain the survival null without any crossover numbers or a sensitivity analysis being presented.

The size of the effect is unknown because the trial ended before it could be measured. Median progression-free survival was not reached with lanreotide within the 96-week fixed study duration, so the delay is known only to exceed the observation window, and the 96-week design cannot address how long treatment should continue.

Progression-free survival and time to tumour progression return the identical 18.0-month placebo median from different event counts (60 against 58), which shows the median sits in a sparse region of the curve where two events make no difference to the estimate.

The chromogranin A result is reported on 64 of 101 and 64 of 103 patients, roughly two-thirds of each arm, with no account of the missing third, and it is a biochemical change in a non-functioning tumour population where it carries no symptomatic meaning.

Enrolment required somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy uptake of grade 2 or higher within the previous 6 months, so the trial selected the patients most likely to respond and says nothing about receptor-poor disease, which is precisely the group in whom embolisation, chemotherapy or resection is being weighed.

The trial excluded any prior radionuclide therapy at any time, chemoembolisation or chemotherapy within 6 months, and more than 15 days of previous somatostatin analogue. The cohort is therefore essentially naive to liver-directed treatment, and nothing in the result informs sequencing with embolisation, radioembolisation or PRRT.

The discussion raises the obvious reading of its own data, that an 18-month placebo median supports watchful waiting, and sets it aside on the ground that the study examined prevention of progression. That is a restatement of the trial's design, not an answer to the question of whether delaying treatment costs the patient anything.

The adverse events that matter for a surgical population are presented as reassurance. Cholelithiasis occurred in 10% against 3% and hyperglycaemia in 5% against 0%, and the serious treatment-related events in the lanreotide arm include biliary fistula and cholelithiasis, in patients who may later need hepatectomy or arterial therapy; the discussion calls the safety profile favourable by comparison with targeted agents and chemotherapy.

The sponsor controlled the trial end to end. Ipsen, which markets lanreotide, designed, funded and conducted the study; the contract research organisation's statisticians worked under the oversight of the sponsor's own biostatistics department; a medical writer paid by the sponsor drafted the manuscript; and one co-author is affiliated to Ipsen.

Two letters in the New England Journal of Medicine with an author reply are linked to this paper in PubMed (PMIDs 25317882, 25317883 and 25317881). The full texts could not be obtained, so no point above draws on them and whatever objections they raise are not represented here.
25014687.n: 204 patients with unresectable or metastatic, somatostatin-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 (Ki-67 under 10%) non-functioning enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours randomised at 48 centres in 14 countries between June 2006 and April 2013: 101 to lanreotide Autogel 120 mg and 103 to placebo, with 96% having had no documented progression in the preceding 3 to 6 months.
25014687.bottom_line: CLARINET establishes that lanreotide 120 mg delays radiographic progression in somatostatin-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, with a hazard ratio of 0.47 and 65% versus 33% progression-free at 24 months, and it does so across hepatic tumour volumes above and below 25%. What it does not establish is that this changes anything a patient feels or how long they live: overall survival and quality of life were identical, the population was non-functioning and 96% radiographically stable at entry, and the grade 2 subgroup confidence interval crosses 1. The placebo arm ran a median 18.0 months without progression, which is the figure to carry into any discussion of whether to start treatment now or watch, and the hepatic-volume subgroup everyone quotes was collapsed from five prespecified categories to two after the data were in.
25014687.funding: Supported by Ipsen, which designed, funded and conducted the study in collaboration with the European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society and the UK and Ireland Neuroendocrine Tumour Society. The blinded database was held by a third-party contract research organisation whose statisticians performed the analyses under the oversight of the sponsor's biostatistics department; a professional medical writer paid by the sponsor, with Watermeadow Medical, assisted in drafting the manuscript, and one co-author is affiliated to Ipsen. Individual disclosure forms were filed separately and do not appear in the article text.

limitations: The design is retrospective.

Type 2 statistical error is possible: the numbers in some groups are too small to show a significant difference where one exists, and considering multiple variables fragments already small subgroups further.

Most patients continued octreotide LAR after resection, especially after publication of PROMID, and the authors state this consistent postoperative use may have contributed to the longer progression-free survival they report.
The small number of patients not given octreotide LAR may be why no difference was seen when octreotide use was tested as a variable.
Successful resection of the primary tumour in 92% of patients may also have contributed to the improved liver progression-free and disease-specific survival.
It is difficult to compare outcomes between published series, so the claim that these figures are better than others' is made with that caveat.
No data support the use of somatostatin analogues after complete resection; the authors frame this as a foundation for future adjuvant studies rather than current evidence.
Several series, including this one, find that the extent of hepatic and extrahepatic disease is underestimated preoperatively in about 15% of cases (19% here).
critique: The cohort cannot test the threshold it was built to test, because it contains no sub-70% arm. The methods state the surgeon did not perform resection in patients in whom 70% debulking was not achievable, so every patient analysed was already filtered for technical feasibility, and the number explored and turned down is never given. The comparison actually made is 70-89% against 90-99% and 100%.

Equivalence is inferred from null results in very small groups. The 70-89% band holds 11 patients and 3 progression events, and P=.95 for progression, P=.74 for liver progression-free survival and P=.37 for disease-specific survival are read as showing no detrimental effect. No equivalence margin and no power calculation appear anywhere.

Liver progression means something different in each debulking group. Progression was scored by RECIST 1.1, which requires measurable target lesions at baseline; the 19 patients resected to 100% have no residual target lesion, so their only route to progression is a new lesion, while the 70-89% group carries measurable residual tumour that can grow. The endpoint is therefore easier to reach in the groups the paper wants to defend.

The exposure variable is the operating surgeon's own unblinded intraoperative eyeball-and-ultrasound estimate recorded at the end of the operation, with no volumetric imaging verification and no second observer. The same surgeon decided who was operated on at all and the percentage each patient was assigned to.

Median follow-up was 37.4 months, roughly half the median liver progression-free survival of 71.6 months (95% CI 56.0 to 87.3). The 90% five-year disease-specific survival, the 88% five-year overall survival and the 85% five-year progression-free rate in older patients are all extrapolations beyond the median follow-up, and no figure in the paper reports numbers at risk.

All 26 comparisons in Tables II and III are unadjusted log-rank tests on 15 progression events and an unstated number of deaths. No multivariable model was fitted at all, so the single surviving finding, age, is unadjusted, and no correction for 26 tests is applied.

The age cutoff of 50 years is not prespecified and does not fall out of the data presented, where the group means were 52.0 and 60.1 years. A dichotomy chosen after seeing a continuous difference then supplies the paper's headline prognostic factor.

Intermediate-grade metastases point consistently the wrong way and are dismissed: P=.07 for progression in Table I, P=.10 for progression-free survival and P=.06 for disease-specific survival, all adverse, on 15 of 45 patients. From those three near-misses the paper advises against sampling multiple liver lesions for grading before debulking.

The grade comparison rests on far fewer specimens than the claim implies. Primary tumours were available in only 22 of 52 patients, so 'all primaries reviewed were low grade' is a statement about 22 specimens, and the primary-versus-metastasis comparison is made in 21 patients.
The number of metastases graded is reported two ways: more than 200 from 45 patients in the results, more than 220 from 46 patients in the discussion.

Figures disagree with text on the paper's own headline. The 5-year liver progression-free survival under age 50 is 25.7% in the results and 21.6% in the Figure 3 legend, and the age disease-specific survival P value is .03 in the abstract and Table III but .025 in the results.

No operative mortality and no morbidity rate appear anywhere in the paper. For a series whose entire argument is that more patients should be offered this operation, the only harm datum reported is a median length of stay of 6 days.

The number of deaths is never stated. A 90% five-year disease-specific survival and an 88% overall survival are reported without the event count behind them, and the statement that all deaths were from liver failure cannot be checked against a denominator.

Octreotide exposure is tangled up with calendar time. The cohort was operated between 2007 and 2011 and the authors say postoperative octreotide LAR became routine after PROMID appeared in 2009, so the most-treated patients are also the most recently operated and the least followed. No period analysis is presented.

Six patients underwent a second liver debulking and two who progressed were enrolled in RADIANT-4 (everolimus versus placebo). Disease-specific survival therefore reflects salvage treatment that the analysis does not model, and liver progression is itself the trigger for that salvage, as the author confirmed at the podium that other modalities are withheld until liver progression occurs.

The conclusion that extrahepatic disease does not matter rests on 37 months of median follow-up in a disease where extrahepatic carcinoid kills over many years. Eighteen patients were left with unresected extrahepatic disease, no patient died of it in the observation window, and that null result (P=.45 and P=.57) is turned into advice to offer debulking regardless of extrahepatic resectability.

At the published discussion Sareh Parangi argued that because much of the extrahepatic disease here was found at operation, prospectively selecting patients with known extrahepatic disease would be a different population; the author's answer, that two-thirds of the 34 were known preoperatively, concedes that a third were not. Allan Siperstein made the related point that the paper reports debulking in isolation from the multimodality therapy these patients actually receive.

The senior author declares consultancy for Novartis Oncology, which markets octreotide LAR and everolimus, and for Pfizer, which markets sunitinib, and the discussion attributes part of the series' unusually long progression-free survival to octreotide LAR. Funding came from the institution's own carcinoid research foundation. A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so the only external appraisal is the printed podium discussion.
25456912.n: 52 patients with carcinoid liver metastases debulked by a single surgeon between January 2007 and December 2011; the number explored and then not resected because 70% debulking was judged unachievable is never reported.
25456912.bottom_line: This is the source of the 70% debulking threshold, and what it shows is that among patients in whom a single surgeon judged intraoperatively that at least 70% of visible liver disease could be removed, the amount actually removed made no measurable difference to liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), while 5-year disease-specific survival was 90% and the only surviving predictor was age under 50. It does not show that 70% is a defensible floor, because the design excluded every patient in whom 70% was not achievable, so there is no sub-70% comparison and no count of how many were explored and declined. The null results that justify the expanded criteria rest on 11 patients in the lowest band, 15 progression events, 26 unadjusted log-rank tests and a median follow-up half the length of the median endpoint.
25456912.funding: OHSU Carcinoid Research Foundation; R. Pommier declares consultancy for Novartis Oncology Pharmaceuticals and Pfizer.

limitations: The paper has no limitations section; the concessions below are made in the discussion.

Overall survival data are immature: the first interim analysis suggested only a trend in favour of everolimus and was not statistically significant, and up to two further survival analyses were planned as the data matured.
The authors characterise the effect as a durable benefit in delaying tumour growth rather than as tumour shrinkage.
Most everolimus-related adverse events required dose modification or interruption to manage.
The mTOR rationale rests on indirect evidence, decreased S6 phosphorylation and reduced Ki-67 labelling in earlier translational work, rather than on any biomarker measured in this trial.

The authors present the absence of crossover as the reason their survival estimate is less biased than RADIANT-2's, implicitly conceding that the earlier trial's survival analysis was not interpretable.
critique: The central and local radiology readings disagree by months in both arms: placebo 3.9 against 5.5 months and everolimus 11.0 against 14.0. The authors blame exactly this kind of reader discordance for RADIANT-2's failure, so the size of the effect reported here depends on which read is used, and the stratified central estimate (HR 0.48) differs materially from the unstratified all-patients figure in the forest plot (0.56, 95% CI 0.41-0.77).

The claim of consistency across subgroups is not what the forest plots show. In men the hazard ratio is 0.78 (95% CI 0.51-1.22) against 0.39 (0.25-0.60) in women, and in the better-prognosis stratum A it is 0.63 (0.40-1.02) against 0.43 (0.28-0.66) in stratum B. Two of the trial's own prespecified subgroups therefore fail to exclude no effect, and neither is mentioned in the text.

Stratum A is the stratum that contains the appendiceal, caecal, jejunal, ileal and duodenal primaries, that is the midgut patient a surgeon sees with liver metastases, and that is the stratum in which the confidence interval crosses 1.

The analysis by primary tumour origin that supports the lung and gastrointestinal labels is a retrospective post hoc grouping using unstratified Cox models, with one patient of thymic origin excluded from it, among roughly eighteen subgroup estimates reported without multiplicity adjustment or interaction testing.

Overall survival was tested at its first interim look with 70 deaths against a boundary of 0.0002 and returned a one-sided p of 0.037. Presenting that as a possible trend towards benefit is a description of a result three orders of magnitude from its own threshold, and no mature survival analysis appears in this report.

A 2% confirmed response rate means essentially nobody's tumour shrank by RECIST criteria, so the entire gain is the absence of documented growth over a placebo median of 3.9 months in a disease whose natural history is highly variable.

Best supportive care explicitly excluded somatostatin analogues for tumour control, although 53 to 56% of patients had received one before entry and PROMID and CLARINET had already established them. The comparator is therefore less than the standard of care that existed when the trial reported.

Carcinoid syndrome and all pancreatic primaries were excluded by protocol, and only 23% had an ileal and 8% a jejunal primary, so the trial does not cover the functional small-bowel patient who most often arrives with neuroendocrine liver metastases.

The claim that benefit is independent of the extent of liver metastasis is made in a cohort selected to have very little: 80% had liver metastases and most had 10% or less hepatic tumour burden. The high-burden patient for whom a liver-directed option is in question is barely represented.
Patients embolised within 6 months, or ablated or cryoablated within 2 months, were excluded, so nothing here informs the combination or sequencing of everolimus with liver-directed therapy.

Tolerability is the real counterweight to a 7.1-month median gain: two thirds of patients needed dose reduction or interruption, 12% discontinued for grade 3 or 4 drug-related events, and non-infectious pneumonitis occurred in 16%. No quality-of-life result is reported in this paper at all.
The 2:1 allocation leaves only 97 patients on placebo, so every subgroup comparison divides a control arm of under a hundred patients.
Response and progression were assessed by modified RECIST version 1.0 in a trial enrolling in 2012 and 2013, when RECIST 1.1 was the established standard.

The funder co-designed the trial, a funder-designated contract research organisation collected the data, the funder's statistical team performed the analysis, and the first draft was written by the first author with a medical writer employed by the funder; two co-authors are affiliated to Novartis.

A linked comment (Oberg, 'Universal everolimus for malignant neuroendocrine tumours?', Lancet 2016;387:924-926, PMID 26703890) and correspondence specifically about ileal tumours (Walter and Lombard-Bohas, Lancet 2016;388:236, PMID 27479567, with authors' reply PMID 27479568) accompany this paper. None of those texts was accessible, so no position is attributed to them here, though the correspondence title indicates the ileal subgroup was contested at the time.
26703889.n: 302 patients with advanced, progressive, non-functional, well-differentiated grade 1 or 2 neuroendocrine tumours of lung or gastrointestinal origin, randomised 2:1 at 97 centres in 25 countries between April 2012 and August 2013: 205 to everolimus 10 mg daily and 97 to placebo. Eighty per cent had liver metastases, most with 10% or less hepatic tumour burden, and crossover was not permitted.
26703889.bottom_line: RADIANT-4 is the basis for using everolimus in advanced, progressive, non-functional lung and gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumours, almost tripling median progression-free survival from 3.9 to 11.0 months by blinded central review, in a population that had virtually no proven systemic option. The gain is stabilisation and not shrinkage, with a 2% response rate, no mature survival data, and two thirds of patients needing dose reduction or interruption, 12% stopping for toxicity and pneumonitis in 16%. The consistency across subgroups that the paper asserts does not hold for men (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.51-1.22) or for the better-prognosis stratum containing the ileal and jejunal primaries (0.63, 0.40-1.02), and with 80% of patients carrying 10% or less hepatic burden and recent embolisation or ablation excluded, the trial says nothing about the heavily liver-burdened patient.
26703889.funding: Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corporation.
