The study was designed by academic investigators together with representatives of the funder; data were collected electronically through a contract research organisation designated by the funder (PPD Global Ltd) and analysed by the funder's statistical team; the first draft was prepared by the first author with a medical writer employed by the funder. Two co-authors are affiliated to Novartis. The declaration of interests records honoraria, consulting or advisory fees and research funding from Novartis for the first author and most senior co-authors, alongside Ipsen, Lexicon and Italfarmaco.

limitations: The main limitation is that treatment could not be randomised, and segregation of the groups on criteria other than those applied might occur in a non-randomised study.
Some clinical aspects that led to the final enlistment decision might have been underestimated, which is why propensity-score adjustment was adopted.
The sample was too small for conventional propensity-score matching, so the score could only be entered as a covariate in the regression models.
The prognostic-factor analysis is explicitly exploratory because it was not possible to satisfy the ten-events-per-variable rule.

Histology in 11 non-transplant patients (24% of that group) was assessed only on the primary tumour because liver metastatic tissue was unavailable; the authors call this an unavoidable bias incorporated into the regression models.
More intense systemic therapy, including peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy, was given to the non-transplant patients, a bias the authors describe as inherent to field practice.
The study was conducted in the pre-molecular-target era of NET treatment, so transplantation after downstaging with newer agents remains uninvestigated.
Quality of life was not measured over time; the authors infer it from the rate of long-term curability.
The survival benefit observed might be due both to the transplant itself and to the selection of patients for transplantation.
The authors state that randomised studies in this setting are considered infeasible, and that uniform objective criteria for selecting transplant candidates upfront are still lacking.
critique: The propensity score does not adjust for the imbalances the paper itself identifies. Backward AIC selection reduced the model to year of diagnosis, age, T stage and serum chromogranin, so WHO 2010 grade, percentage liver involvement, primary site, carcinoid syndrome and locoregional or systemic treatment, all of which were offered to the model, are absent from the adjustment that produces the headline hazard ratio of 7.4.

Four non-transplant patients (8.7%) were reclassified as G3 on WHO 2010 review and none of the transplanted patients were (p=0.032). G3 histology is itself an exclusion criterion of the Milan-NET rule set, so the comparator arm contains patients who do not meet the criteria the study exists to validate, and the adjustment does not remove them.

Seven patients breached the liver-burden criterion in the same way: H3 disease, over 50% of the parenchyma, in 4 transplanted and 3 non-transplanted patients, with liver involvement undetermined in a further 3 non-transplant patients, against an inclusion rule of under 50%.

Hilar nodal status, which the same group's later work finds to be the only independent predictor of post-transplant outcome, is unknown in 40 of the 46 non-transplant patients (86.9%) and known in 37 of 42 transplanted patients. The two arms cannot be compared on it, and the paper reports the p value of 0.645 as if they could.

Time-to-progression means a different thing in each arm. After total hepatectomy there is no measurable liver lesion, so a transplanted patient can only have an event by growing a new one, while a non-transplant patient has measurable residual metastases that need only enlarge by the RECIST threshold. A 13.1% versus 89% difference is partly an artefact of that asymmetry.

The comparator arm was systematically denied surgery. The text states that none of the non-transplant patients was considered for palliative cytoreductive liver resection, even though 75 of the original 280 referrals were excluded precisely because their disease was resectable. Transplantation is therefore being compared with medical therapy, not with the best available surgical alternative.

The non-transplant backbone is thin even for its era: 89.1% on somatostatin analogues, 13.0% chemoembolisation, 8.7% peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy and 2.2% targeted agents. A 10-year survival of 22.4% is the yardstick, and it reflects what was withheld as much as what transplantation adds.

Treatment is unbalanced in the other direction too, and this is never adjusted for: the transplant group received TACE in 40.5% versus 13.0%, and somatostatin analogues in 54.8% versus 89.1%, so the two arms differ in liver-directed therapy before the index procedure as well as after it.

Transplant recipients were a median of 15 years younger (40.5 versus 55.5 years), and the paper's own multivariable analysis makes age an independent determinant of death, with hazard ratios of 3.41 and 3.72 for patients younger than 42 and older than 54 against the 42-54 band. The discussion concedes the tendency to push for transplantation in the young, which is the mechanism by which age and treatment became confounded.

The Cox models use left truncation to handle delayed entry, but the Kaplan-Meier curves, the 5- and 10-year survival percentages and the difference-in-mean-survival-time benefit calculation are not stated to do so. Transplanted patients had to survive a median of 18.5 months from primary resection to reach their transplant, and the headline 97.2% and 88.8% are measured from primary resection.

The propensity model discriminates almost too well. A bootstrap-corrected Harrell C of 0.861 means the two groups are nearly separable on baseline characteristics, so there is little region of common support; combined with the authors' own admission that matching was impossible, the covariate adjustment is being asked to bridge groups that barely overlap.

The paper's own benefit figure falls short of the benchmark it invokes. The discussion argues that transplant benefit justifies MELD exception points by noting that a MELD of 15 corresponds to 12 months of life gained at 5 years, while the adjusted 5-year benefit reported here is 6.82 months with a confidence interval running down to 1.10 months. Only the 10-year figure clears that bar.

No perioperative harm of transplantation is reported anywhere. Grafts were marginal in 88% of cases, with a median donor age of 65, 40% steatosis and a donor risk index of 1.6, and the paper gives no 90-day mortality, no graft loss or retransplantation rate, no rejection rate and no cause of death for the 5 deaths in the transplant group.

Allocation ran on exactly the variables that predict outcome. Of the 46 non-transplant patients, 24 could not be listed because of waiting-list conditions and 22 refused, 18 of them because they judged their own health normal enough to postpone transplant indefinitely. That self-selection puts the better-feeling patients in the comparator arm, which argues against the result, but it also means the groups were formed by patient disposition and list capacity rather than by any measured clinical variable the propensity score could capture.

Only 88 of 280 referrals (31%) met the criteria, at a national cancer institute operating a bespoke protocol with its own regional organ-sharing agreement since 1995. The 88.8% ten-year survival is the output of that selection machine and says little about what a general transplant programme would achieve.

Missing data were handled by substitution rather than modelled: categorical values replaced by the modal category and continuous values by the median wherever missingness was under 10%, in a dataset with 10.9% missing T stage, 13.0% Nx, 15.2% missing grade and 86.9% unknown hilar nodes in the non-transplant arm.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment on this paper, so no independent appraisal of the benefit estimate accompanies it in the literature.
27134017.n: 88 patients meeting the Milan-NET criteria, drawn from 280 consecutive referrals with gastroenteropancreatic NET liver metastases between June 1995 and January 2010; 42 were transplanted and 46 continued non-transplant treatment, with a median follow-up of 122 months in both groups.
27134017.bottom_line: This is the paper that fixes the Milan-NET criteria and attaches a number to them: under restrictive selection, transplantation was followed by 88.8% ten-year survival and a propensity-adjusted benefit rising from 6.8 months at 5 years to 38.4 months at 10, an outcome no other NET series had reported. It does not establish that transplantation caused that difference, because allocation turned on waiting-list capacity, age and patient refusal rather than disease, the transplant group was 15 years younger, and the comparator arm was given no cytoreductive liver resection, 8.7% PRRT and 2.2% targeted agents. The propensity model that carries the adjustment was reduced by automatic selection to four variables and excludes grade, liver burden and treatment, which are the very imbalances the paper flags in its own results.
27134017.funding: Non-sponsored, academic, investigator-initiated study. V. Mazzaferro supported by grants from INT-Milan on Hepato-Oncology (5x1000 grant), AIRC (Italian Association for Cancer Research) and the National Transplant Centre, Rome. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

limitations: The paper has no limitations section; the concessions below are made in passing in the discussion.

The trial had not reached the point at which median overall survival could be calculated, so the interim analysis only suggests longer survival with 177Lu-Dotatate; the final analysis was still to come, at 158 deaths or 5 years after the last randomisation, whichever came first.
The claim of no renal toxic effects is bounded explicitly by the trial time frame, a median follow-up of 14 months, and depends on concurrent administration of a renal-protective amino acid infusion.

Myelodysplastic syndrome is identified by the authors as an event of particular interest because a long-term risk of myelodysplasia or acute leukaemia of about 2% has been reported previously, and one case had already occurred before the data cutoff, in a patient with pre-existing monoclonal gammopathy.
Most of the nausea and vomiting is attributed to the concurrent amino acid infusion rather than to the radioligand, which the authors note resolved once the infusion finished.
critique: The comparator is a dose escalation nobody expected to work. Octreotide LAR 60 mg every 4 weeks has never been shown to control tumour growth, and the control arm's 8.4-month median progression-free survival is the yardstick against which a 79% risk reduction is measured. Everolimus, chemotherapy and liver-directed therapy, the treatments actually competing for these patients, are not in the trial.

The trial is open-label and the two arms are visibly different, one being a four-cycle intravenous radioligand with amino acid infusion and the other an intramuscular depot. Central blinded radiology protects the progression reading but not the decision to withdraw, the use of rescue octreotide, adverse event reporting or the choice of subsequent therapy, all of which were made by unblinded investigators.

The interim survival result is presented as encouraging against a threshold it did not come close to meeting. Fourteen deaths against 26 give a hazard ratio of 0.40 at p=0.004, while the prespecified O'Brien-Fleming boundary at that analysis was 0.000085. The discussion's statement that the results suggest longer overall survival travelled into guidelines and practice well before the final analysis, which was negative.

The response analysis quietly loses 27 patients. Objective response is reported on 101 and 100 evaluable patients against 116 and 113 randomised, with no account of who was excluded or why, and the 18% rate comprises one complete and 17 partial responses.

Nearly a quarter of the treated patients did not complete the regimen. Of 116 randomised to 177Lu-Dotatate, 111 received at least one dose, 77% received all four cycles and 8 required dose reduction, so the progression-free survival benefit is attached to a variable exposure that is never analysed by cycles received or administered activity.

Renal injury and secondary myeloid malignancy are the two harms that decide whether PRRT is worth giving, and both are late. A median follow-up of 14 months cannot see them. The supporting creatinine data sit in supplementary figures, and the single myelodysplastic syndrome case is attributed partly to a pre-existing monoclonal gammopathy.

Eligibility required Krenning grade 2 to 4 uptake in every target lesion on planar scintigraphy with central confirmation, so any patient with one receptor-poor metastasis was excluded. Receptor heterogeneity is the main reason PRRT fails in practice, and the trial selected it out.

The trial excludes everything that would place PRRT in a treatment sequence: no prior PRRT at all, and no surgery, liver-directed transarterial therapy or chemotherapy within 12 weeks. Nothing here says whether PRRT works after embolisation, or whether embolisation works after PRRT.

Eighty-three to 84% of patients had liver metastases and the primary report contains no analysis by hepatic tumour burden, the variable that most determines whether a liver-directed option competes with PRRT in this population. That analysis appeared only in later post hoc publications.

Patients in both arms could receive subcutaneous octreotide rescue injections for carcinoid symptoms, and the amount used is not reported. The control arm was on twice the depot dose, so any symptom comparison between the arms is confounded by both the rescue medication and the depot dose.

Enrolment averaged under two patients per centre per year across 41 centres over three and a half years, so almost every site contributed a handful of patients to a trial whose procedure requires nuclear medicine infrastructure.

The sponsor designed, funded, monitored and analysed the trial. Advanced Accelerator Applications designed it in collaboration with the last two authors, contract research organisations collected, compiled, maintained and analysed the data, a sponsor-funded medical writer assisted with the first draft, and two co-authors are affiliated to the company in France and the USA.

Four correspondence items are linked to this paper in PubMed, three letters and the authors' reply (PMIDs 28382815, 28379809, 28382816 and 28379808). None of their full texts was obtained, so whatever objections they raise are not represented here.
28076709.n: 229 patients with well-differentiated, somatostatin-receptor-positive, inoperable midgut neuroendocrine tumours progressing on octreotide LAR, randomised 1:1 at 41 centres in 8 countries between September 2012 and January 2016: 116 to 177Lu-Dotatate plus octreotide LAR 30 mg and 113 to octreotide LAR 60 mg. 111 patients received at least one dose of 177Lu-Dotatate and 77% received all four; response was evaluable in 101 and 100.
28076709.bottom_line: NETTER-1 is the trial that made peptide receptor radionuclide therapy standard second-line treatment for midgut neuroendocrine tumours, with a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.21 and an 18% response rate against 3%, by blinded central review. What it establishes is superiority over octreotide LAR 60 mg, a dose escalation with no antitumour pedigree, in a narrowly selected population: midgut primary, Ki-67 at or below 20%, Krenning grade 2 to 4 uptake in every target lesion, and documented progression on standard-dose somatostatin analogue. It establishes nothing about survival, since the interim p value of 0.004 fell far short of the prespecified 0.000085 boundary and the final analysis five years later was negative, and nothing about the late renal and myeloid harms, which cannot be seen at a median follow-up of 14 months.
28076709.funding: Supported by Advanced Accelerator Applications, which sponsored the trial and designed it in collaboration with the last two authors. Contract research organisations monitored the trial and collected, compiled, maintained and analysed the data, and the first draft was prepared by the first author with assistance from a professional medical writer funded by the sponsor. Two co-authors are affiliated to Advanced Accelerator Applications in St Genis-Pouilly, France and the USA; individual disclosure forms were filed separately and do not appear in the article text.

limitations: The panel records many areas of non-consensus, including whether to treat or observe low-volume asymptomatic metastatic disease, octreotide versus lanreotide, whether to continue a somatostatin analogue past progression, which embolisation modality to prefer, how to select patients for carcinoid heart disease screening, and whether surveillance should extend beyond 10 years.
There is no high-quality evidence favouring any liver-directed therapy over another or over systemic treatment.

The cumulative hepatic radiation burden of radioembolisation followed by PRRT is unstudied, and the panel names RETNET (NCT02724540) as the trial needed to resolve the comparison between embolisation techniques.
Roughly half the panel judged chromogranin A, pancreastatin and neuron-specific enolase too prone to false positive and false negative results to recommend.
Most panellists judged the evidence insufficient to use embolisation as second-line therapy.
Surgical management, including the hepatic debulking threshold, was deliberately excluded and deferred to the companion surgical guideline.
critique: Consensus here is a show of hands. Fifteen panellists voted by audience response system, consensus was defined as no more than one oppositional vote and significant majority as 75% agreement, and no systematic review, evidence table or grading system exists. A near-unanimous statement and an even split appear in the same typography, so the strength behind a recommendation cannot be read off the page.

The declared interests mirror the evidence base almost exactly. Panellists report advisory, speaker or institutional research relationships with Novartis, Ipsen, Lexicon and Advanced Accelerator Applications, the makers of the somatostatin analogues, telotristat and the radioligand the guideline recommends, and the panel's interventional radiologist declares research grants from Guerbet and BTG, consultancy for Guerbet, Terumo, Merit Medical and Bayer and proctoring for Sirtex while the panel votes on embolisation modality.

The second-line endorsement of 177Lu-DOTATATE rests on NETTER-1's progression-free survival report. The final overall survival analysis published four years later was negative (hazard ratio 0.84, p=0.30), so the '79% improvement' quoted here is a progression figure and carries no survival claim.

The recommendation to try somatostatin analogues regardless of the receptor imaging result sits awkwardly beside the same guideline's receptor-based selection for PRRT, and no evidence of benefit in receptor-negative midgut disease is offered.

Roughly ten years of surveillance with cross-sectional imaging, every 6 months in the first year then annually, is recommended on a recurrence rate of about 50% with no evidence that earlier detection of recurrence changes outcome, and with no consideration of cumulative radiation exposure or cost in a disease whose patients live for decades.

The telotristat recommendation prefers a new drug to dose escalation of an existing one without any head-to-head comparison, on the strength of a 35% reduction in daily bowel movements at the higher of two doses in a short symptom trial.

Carcinoid heart disease screening is triggered at a 5-HIAA above five times normal, a threshold given without any diagnostic accuracy data, in the same breath as the panel reporting that it could not agree on how to select patients for screening at all.

The question that matters most to a liver tumour board, which embolisation technique to use, produced no consensus, and the trial the panel nominated to settle it later closed its drug-eluting-bead arm for excess severe complications. The uncertainty recorded here was real and was eventually resolved on safety grounds rather than efficacy.

Splitting the surgical and medical guidance into companion papers means neither document addresses sequencing between them: this paper defers debulking to the surgical companion while recommending PRRT and embolisation, and the surgical paper recommends cytoreduction without reference to the systemic sequence.
No funding statement appears anywhere in the document.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
28609356.n: No patient cohort. A 15-member multidisciplinary panel voted by audience response system, with consensus defined as no more than one oppositional vote and significant majority as agreement of at least 75%.
28609356.bottom_line: This is the medical counterpart to the NANETS surgical guideline, and its firm positions are narrow: surveillance for about a decade after resection, somatostatin-receptor imaging at baseline but not for routine follow-up, 177Lu-DOTATATE as second line after progression on a somatostatin analogue, and telotristat rather than dose escalation for refractory carcinoid diarrhoea. On the questions a liver tumour board brings, it records no consensus at all: whether to treat or observe low-volume asymptomatic metastases, which embolisation modality to use, and whether to continue a somatostatin analogue past progression. The document carries no evidence grading, its PRRT endorsement predates NETTER-1's negative survival analysis, and nearly every panellist declares relationships with the manufacturers of the drugs and devices under discussion.
28609356.funding: No funding statement appears. Declared interests are extensive: J.R. Strosberg reports advisory boards for Novartis, Ipsen and Lexicon, speaker's bureaux for Ipsen and Lexicon and institutional research funding from Advanced Accelerator Applications and Novartis; J.A. Chan, P.L. Kunz, E. Bergsland, T.R. Halfdanarson, R.F. Pommier, J.C. Yao, E.S. and J.S.Z. report consulting, advisory, speaker or institutional research relationships with Novartis, Ipsen, Lexicon, Advanced Accelerator Applications, Dicerna, Esanex, Genentech, Merck, Oxigene and Thermo Fisher; M.C. Soulen reports research grants from Guerbet and BTG International, consultancy for Guerbet, Terumo, Merit Medical and Bayer and proctoring for Sirtex Medical; R.S. reports advisory board and a research grant from BTG. The remaining authors declare no conflict of interest.

limitations: The authors state that the lack of randomised trials makes it difficult to prove the validity of these clinical recommendations, and that no randomised trial defines the surgical treatment of these tumours or is likely ever to be performed.
The recommendations are presented as based on clinical experience and a careful review of the literature rather than on graded evidence.
The historic 90% debulking figure is conceded to have come from an observation about symptom relief and never to have been validated as an oncologic threshold.

The survival advantage claimed for resecting the primary tumour in the presence of inoperable liver metastases comes from retrospective cohorts and the authors acknowledge that selection bias cannot be excluded.
The panel records near consensus, that is one or two dissenting votes, on several questions including those about the debulking threshold.
The literature is conceded not to support prophylactic octreotide for carcinoid crisis, although an intraoperative infusion is sanctioned as harmless practice.
critique: There is no systematic search and no grading anywhere in the document. Participants were each assigned one or two questions to research, the panel voted by audience response system, and consensus was defined after the fact as unanimity. No evidence table, risk-of-bias assessment or evidence level accompanies any of the 19 answers, so a statement resting on three retrospective series and one resting on panel practice look identical on the page.

The 70% threshold was set by the centres that proposed it. Both single-institution series behind it come from institutions represented on the panel, and the lead author's and the Oregon group's own work supplies the central number, with the conference itself hosted by one of those institutions.

One of those supporting series cannot test the threshold at all, because it excluded by design every patient in whom 70% debulking was judged intraoperatively unachievable and so contains no sub-70% arm. In that series the extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), and age was the only predictor.

The 'over 70% versus under 70%' comparison quoted here, overall survival not reached against 6.5 years and progression-free survival 3.2 against 1.3 years, therefore comes from a cohort in which the sub-70% group is a selected residue of patients in whom more could not be removed, which is a statement about resectability rather than about the benefit of a threshold.

The absence of a survival difference between R0 and R1 or R2 resection is used to justify debulking, and it is derived from retrospective series in which margin status was determined by what the disease allowed rather than by allocation. Patients who end up R2 are those whose tumour could not be cleared.

Open laparotomy with digital palpation of the entire small bowel is recommended because 25 to 44% of these tumours are multifocal, with no evidence that finding and removing the additional subcentimetre primaries changes survival. The recommendation against purely laparoscopic resection rests entirely on that surrogate.

The contraindications to cytoreduction are given without derivation. Liver replacement above 50% to 70% is a twenty-point band presented as a threshold, and grade 3 histology and poor performance status are excluded on judgement rather than on any cited comparison of operated with non-operated patients in those groups.
Ten of the thirteen participants are surgeons, deliberating on whether surgery should be offered to more patients and at a lower threshold than before.

Prophylactic cholecystectomy at the index operation is recommended on gallstone rates of 52 to 63% during somatostatin analogue therapy, with no figure for how often those stones become symptomatic or need intervention and no estimate of the added morbidity of the extra procedure.

No conflict-of-interest statement of any kind appears in this paper, although its NANETS companion guideline published in the same issue of the same journal carries extensive industry disclosures for several of the same authors, including Bergsland, Strosberg and Pommier.

The conference was organised at the lead author's institution with acknowledgement of that institution's NIH SPORE grant in neuroendocrine tumours, and that institution's own series underpins the document's central recommendation.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so the lowering of the debulking threshold from 90% to 70% entered surgical practice without published external appraisal.
28609357.n: No patient cohort. A consensus conference at the University of Iowa on 11 and 12 August 2016 with ten surgeons plus a gastroenterologist, a radiologist and a nuclear medicine physician, answering 19 predefined questions; each participant researched one or two questions and the panel voted by audience response system.
28609357.bottom_line: This is the document that moved the hepatic debulking threshold in small bowel NET from 90% to 70% and that licenses cytoreduction regardless of the number or size of metastases, intermediate grade, positive margins or extrahepatic disease, together with resection of the primary even when the liver disease is inoperable. Every one of those positions rests on retrospective single-institution series, two of them from centres represented on the panel, with no systematic search, no evidence grading and no randomised data, which the authors concede will never exist. The specific weakness worth remembering is that the series most often cited for the 70% figure excluded by design every patient in whom 70% was unachievable, and within it the extent of debulking predicted neither progression nor death.
28609357.funding: No funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration appears. The acknowledgements thank the conference organisers, M. Sue O'Dorisio and the Iowa SPORE grant in neuroendocrine tumours (NIH P50 CA174521-01), and the leadership of NANETS for providing the impetus for the conference.

limitations: Retrospective single-centre design, so inherent selection bias must be considered.
The influence of tumour progression on the serologic toxicities was not taken into account; the authors argue it was likely low because only 4 patients had progressive disease.
Therapies received before or after radioembolisation may have contributed to the long-term toxicities, and assessing their precise contribution remains challenging.
Information on the 42 patients who died was incomplete because most died at outside hospitals, and cause of death could not be definitively determined for all of them.
It is challenging to differentiate the normal radiographic changes that follow radioembolisation from true cirrhosis.

The authors state that further research is needed on risk factors for cirrhosis and portal hypertension in this setting, including baseline characteristics, prior therapy and absorbed liver doses in tumour and non-tumour tissue, none of which this study provides.
Prospective investigation is acknowledged to be difficult given the rarity of the disease and the heterogeneity of these patients.
critique: The argument that dismisses tumour progression as a cause of the liver enzyme rises uses the wrong denominator. The four patients with progressive disease are the four scored at one year among the 52 still being followed; 42 of the 93 patients died and median survival was 28.0 months, so progression in this cohort was common and the stated reason for not adjusting for it does not hold.

The long-term toxicity finding is measured in exactly the patients least damaged by treatment. Of 93 patients, 18 died and 23 were lost before one year, leaving 52 at one year and 11 at four. Sustained ALP and AST elevation beyond four years is therefore a statement about 11 survivors, and the patients whose livers failed fastest are absent from the denominator.

The four-year analysis is a repeated-measures ANOVA over five time points in 11 patients across a panel of serologic tests, with no correction for multiple outcomes, and the significant values are driven by extreme observations: the four-year mean ALP is 224.6 IU/L with a standard deviation of 195.1.

The conclusion that bilobar treatment carries a trend toward treatment-related portal hypertension rests on comparisons that reach significance nowhere: cirrhosis-like morphology 6 of 29 versus 1 of 23 (p=0.093), ascites 5 versus 1, splenomegaly 6 versus 3. The imaging features were also scored without blinding to which lobes had been treated, which is visible on the same scans.

Unilobar and bilobar treatment are not comparable exposures. Bilobar treatment was given because the disease was bilobar, so the group with more enzyme change, more imaging signs of portal hypertension and falling platelets is also the group with more tumour and more total activity.

No dosimetry is reported. Absorbed dose to tumour and to uninvolved liver is absent, which the authors themselves identify as needed, and the null result for total administered activity (HR 1.03, p=0.926) therefore cannot distinguish absence of a dose-response from absence of dose data.

The nine patients who received systemic therapy during the first year included seven on everolimus, a drug that itself raises transaminases and alkaline phosphatase. The toxicity endpoint of this paper is exactly that, and no adjustment or sensitivity analysis excludes them.

A safety study cannot say whether any patient died of liver injury, because cause of death was undeterminable for most of the 42 deaths. 'No radioembolisation-induced liver failure' is a statement about events the authors could observe, in a cohort whose deaths mostly occurred elsewhere.

Median follow-up of 15.0 months is about half the median survival of 28.0 months, whose confidence interval runs from 16.2 to 39.8 months, so the survival estimate spans two years of uncertainty and the prognostic subgroup medians (58.0 and 53.8 months) lie far beyond the observation period.

The multivariable model is over-specified for its event count. On 42 deaths it fits ascites, extrahepatic metastases and an interaction term between them, yielding a hazard ratio of 5.25 with a confidence interval from 1.85 to 14.96 from a small number of patients with baseline ascites.

Baseline ascites is a near-universal contraindication to radioembolisation elsewhere, and those patients had a median survival of 7.3 months (95% CI 3.8-10.2). The paper treats this as a prognostic observation and never asks whether they should have been treated.
The efficacy figure is reported without criteria. The 25% partial response rate at one year names no RECIST or mRECIST version, no central or blinded read, and is computed only in the 52 survivors.

Tumour differentiation was unknown in 22 patients (24%), the cohort is split by the obsolete carcinoid versus islet cell distinction, and no Ki-67 or WHO grade appears anywhere, so nothing here can be stratified by the variable that now drives treatment selection.

The comparison with the glass-microsphere literature is informal and self-serving: the paper notes that rates of cirrhosis-like morphology and portal hypertension were higher in the published TheraSphere cohort, concedes that device, dosimetry or follow-up duration could explain it, and still concludes that its own data support the relative long-term safety of resin microspheres.
Eight segmental and 160 lobar treatments are pooled throughout, although segmental treatment spares far more parenchyma and is the exposure least likely to cause the late changes under study.

No study funding statement appears. The disclosure block lists extensive industry relationships for three authors, including personal fees from Guerbet and Bayer and grants from Terumo and Guerbet to the corresponding author, and none with the manufacturer of the resin microspheres under study. A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment on this paper.
29724520.n: 93 patients (47 women, 46 men, mean age 59) with unresectable NET liver metastases treated with resin yttrium-90 microspheres at one centre between February 2007 and November 2015 across 168 treatments, 48 unilobar and 45 staged bilobar; 52 patients had more than 1 year and only 11 more than 4 years of follow-up.
29724520.bottom_line: This is the best available long-term safety picture for resin yttrium-90 in neuroendocrine liver metastases: alkaline phosphatase and transaminases rise over the first year and are still elevated beyond four, imaging features of cirrhosis-like morphology or portal hypertension appear in 29% at one year, and yet grade 3 serologic toxicity occurred in only 4 of 52 patients and no liver failure was observed. The long-term signal rests on a survivor-selected denominator of 52 patients at one year and 11 at four, with no dosimetry, no adjustment for the seven patients on everolimus, and cause of death unknown in most of the 42 who died. Its most usable finding is prognostic rather than toxicologic: baseline ascites (median survival 7.3 months) or extrahepatic metastases (21.1 months) change the conversation entirely, while patients with neither lived a median of about 5 years.

limitations: No limitations are stated anywhere in the paper; the authors concede only that decades of experience with embolotherapy have left uncertainty about the optimal modality and a paucity of level I evidence, which is why no guideline recommends a specific technique.
The sample-size estimate is acknowledged to rest on existing retrospective studies rather than trial data.
The effect of lipiodol chemoembolisation and drug-eluting-bead chemoembolisation is, in the authors' words, presumed to be equivalent, an assumption made for the power calculation and not tested.
No formal interim efficacy analysis is planned, which the authors justify on the grounds that all three techniques are already in common clinical use.
critique: This paper contains no outcome data at all, and its only quantitative content is the power calculation: median hepatic progression-free survival of 11 months for bland embolisation against 20 months for lipiodol chemoembolisation, taken from retrospective single-centre data in a single reference. Any claim that RETNET showed something about efficacy is a claim about numbers that appear nowhere in it.

The design is a phase II selection study dressed as a definitive comparison. The null hypothesis is equivalence without preconceived ranking, the test is a studentised-range procedure for phase II screening, and the type I error is set at 10% two-sided, so each of the three pairwise comparisons carries a one-in-ten false-positive rate by construction.

The primary endpoint is specified by RECIST 1.0 while eligibility and the secondary progression-free survival endpoint use RECIST 1.1, so the trial's definition of progression differs between the criterion that lets a patient in and the criterion that records an event.

Blinding of the central image review cannot work for one arm. Ethiodised oil is radiographically dense and persists in treated tumour on follow-up CT, so the lipiodol arm is identifiable on the very images the American College of Radiology core is asked to read blind.

The arm-closure trigger is set above the thresholds it cites. The protocol quotes Society of Interventional Radiology benchmarks of 6% for major hepatic complications with an 8% performance threshold and 10% for any complication with a 15% threshold, then sets the stopping rule at a 20% serious-adverse-event rate.

The eligibility criterion is a disjunction that admits patients with no disease activity: uncontrolled symptoms, or RECIST progression, or simply a baseline liver burden above 25%. A patient with 30% burden who is asymptomatic and radiologically stable qualifies, and is then followed for progression-free survival.
Liver tumour burden, both the 25% threshold that confers eligibility and the 70% ceiling that excludes, is assessed by visual estimate rather than volumetry.

Randomisation is stratified only by institution. Grade and primary site are not stratification factors even though a secondary endpoint explicitly compares gut against pancreatic primaries and compares tumour grades, so those comparisons are unstratified and unpowered. Patients with symptomatic but non-progressive disease are to be monitored during accrual to keep allocation balanced, with adjustment as necessary, a procedure the protocol never defines.

Concomitant octreotide is permitted with no protocol control of dose, formulation or timing. Somatostatin analogues have a demonstrated antiproliferative effect on hepatic progression in exactly this population, so an uncontrolled co-intervention acts directly on the primary endpoint.

The clock starts before treatment is finished. Hepatic progression-free survival runs from initial embolotherapy, while additional vascular territories are embolised every 4 weeks up to four treatments per cycle until the whole tumour burden is covered, so patients with more extensive disease accrue follow-up time during months of continuing therapy.

The publication clause hands the funder control of the output: no part of the results may be published or passed to a third party without the consent of the study sponsor, and every investigator is obliged to provide the sponsor with complete test results and all derived data. The grant comes from Guerbet LLC, which manufactures the ethiodised oil that defines one of the three arms, and the senior author consults for that company.

The trial anticipated biliary injury and then selected the particle sizes associated with it. The exclusion list bars choledochoenteric anastomosis, transpapillary stent and papillary sphincterotomy, yet the drug-eluting-bead arm uses 100-300 and 300-500 micrometre beads, the small end implicated in the 54% biloma rate reported in Bhagat's single-centre phase II study, which had already halted its own enrolment.

The accrual assumption is roughly six participants per site per year from at least 16 sites across five countries for a rare tumour requiring three competing interventional techniques to be available and acceptable at every site; no contingency for slower accrual is described beyond an 8% dropout allowance.

The drug-eluting-bead arm was subsequently closed for excess severe complications. That outcome is not in this paper; it is stated in the ENETS 2024 small-intestine guidance (Lamarca et al., PMID 38977327), and no primary report of the closure was available to read, so the detail of how many events in how many patients triggered it cannot be checked here.
30016989.n: No cohort: this is a protocol. 180 patients were planned, 60 per arm, with a target of 194 enrollees assuming 8% dropout, drawn from at least 16 sites over a 24-month accrual period; enrolment opened in March 2017 and was ongoing when the manuscript was submitted.
30016989.bottom_line: This is a protocol and reports no outcome data whatever: it fixes the design of the first randomised comparison of bland embolisation, lipiodol chemoembolisation and drug-eluting-bead chemoembolisation in liver-dominant neuroendocrine metastases, with 60 patients per arm and hepatic progression-free survival by blinded central review as the primary endpoint. Its only numbers are a power calculation assuming 11 months of hepatic progression-free survival after bland embolisation against 20 months after lipiodol chemoembolisation, taken from retrospective single-centre data, with drug-eluting beads simply presumed equivalent to lipiodol. Nothing in it can support a statement about which technique works better, and the trial's actual contribution to practice came from the safety stopping rule that later closed the drug-eluting-bead arm.

Soulen declares research funding from Guerbet LLC and BTG International and consultancy for Guerbet LLC, Merit Medical, Terumo Medical and Bayer/Onyx; the remaining authors declare no competing interests.

limitations: No consensus was reached on hepatic cytoreduction. Over half the panel favoured individualised treatment with a target above 70%, others held that cytoreduction might only be effective if all lesions could be removed, and a few questioned whether any benefit of cytoreduction has been established at all because every supporting study is a retrospective series prone to selection bias. The panel calls this a controversial area where the level of evidence is weak (level 3).
No consensus was reached on resecting the primary tumour in the presence of unresectable metastases; the majority view that it may help in selected cases rests on retrospective data.

The panel states that limitations of the available data constrain the specificity of its recommendations on initial evaluation, extent of follow-up, selection for observation versus resection, and the extent of surgical resection.

The safety of combining major pancreatectomy with major liver debulking in one operation is not entirely clear from the literature, and the panel notes the theoretical risk of hepatic infection through a biliary-enteric anastomosis after pancreaticoduodenectomy.

Most published liver debulking series are dominated by small bowel primaries with only a minority of pancreatic primaries, and complication rates and simultaneous primary resections are inconsistently reported within them.

In the observation-versus-resection literature the panel warns that reporting and selection biases mean caution is needed before reading the results as a uniform endorsement of resection in small pancreatic NET.
The recommendations for well-differentiated grade 3 tumours and for the 1 to 2 cm size window are acknowledged as unsupported pending studies using the 2017 WHO classification.
critique: The recommendation contradicts the data printed immediately above it. The text asserts that studies have shown little difference in progression-free or overall survival once more than 70% cytoreduction is achieved, while the cited series gives progression-free survival of 20.6 months for 70% to 90% against 56.1 months for over 90%, a near-threefold difference. The statistical equivalence that was actually reported applies to overall survival between those two bands, not to progression-free survival.

The 70% threshold is imported from small bowel NET series into pancreatic NET, and the panel itself records that most of the debulking literature consists of small bowel primaries. The number that governs the operation is therefore borrowed from a different disease.

No consensus was reached on either of the two questions that decide a pancreatic NET liver operation, the cytoreduction threshold and resection of the primary in metastatic disease, and the document is nevertheless cited as support for the 70% threshold.

There is no systematic search and no formal grading system. Each participant was assigned two questions to research and the statements combine that personal review with expert opinion, with 'level 3' appearing as a narrative descriptor rather than a grade attached to each recommendation.
Fourteen of the 17 participants are surgeons, deliberating on when surgery should be offered.

The argument that extrahepatic disease should not contraindicate resection, because it is rarely the cause of death, is a prognostic observation from retrospective series with limited follow-up, and it is used to widen operative indications rather than as a statement about what kills these patients over decades.
A nodal yield of 11 to 15 lymph nodes is set as a staging standard with no evidence cited that achieving it changes management or outcome in pancreatic NET.
The suggestion that resecting the primary may improve the response to PRRT is explicitly speculative and is nonetheless listed among the reasons to operate.

Disclosures bear directly on the technical statements. One panellist reports research funding from Intuitive Surgical and travel expenses for a robotics symposium in a document that addresses operative approach, and others report advisory or research relationships with Ipsen, Novartis, Advanced Accelerator Applications, Curium and Lexicon while the panel votes on statements about PRRT and somatostatin analogues.
No funding statement for the conference appears anywhere in the paper.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
31856076.n: No patient cohort. A consensus conference in Iowa City on 19 and 20 July 2018 with 14 surgeons, two radiologists and a gastroenterologist answering 34 predefined questions; each participant researched two questions, and the supporting literature is almost entirely retrospective cohorts described as level 3.
31856076.bottom_line: This is the NANETS surgical reference for pancreatic NET, and on the two questions that matter for liver metastases it reached no consensus: over half the panel favoured an individualised cytoreduction target above 70%, others held that only complete removal helps, and a few doubted that any benefit of cytoreduction has been shown, since every supporting study is retrospective. Its firmer positions are about the primary: observe non-functioning tumours under 1 cm, individualise 1 to 2 cm, resect all functional tumours, clear 11 to 15 nodes, and do not operate on poorly differentiated carcinoma. The specific thing to carry forward is that its own cited data do not support the claim it makes for the 70% threshold, since progression-free survival was 20.6 against 56.1 months for 70-90% versus over 90% debulking, a difference the recommendation text describes as little.
31856076.funding: No funding statement appears for the conference or the paper. Declared interests include a research grant from Mauna Kea Technologies (J.F.T.), research funding from Intuitive Surgical and robotics symposium travel (H.J.Z.), advisory board and consultancy for Curium (T.A.H.), research funds from Novartis (M.K.K.), research funding from Ipsen and Advanced Accelerator Applications (Y.M.), research funding from Ipsen and Thermo Fisher with advisory boards for Ipsen, Curium, Novartis and Lexicon (T.R.H.), consultancy and advisory roles with Crinetics, Ipsen, Novartis and Lexicon plus UpToDate royalties and Merck stock (J.A.C.), and consultancy for Novartis, Lexicon and Advanced Accelerator Applications (R.F.P.); the other authors declare none.

limitations: Only one randomised trial, NETTER-1 in midgut NET, underpins the document; every other recommendation rests on retrospective and registry data.
Overall survival data were preliminary at the time of writing and the final analysis was pending, so the survival case for PRRT was unproven even in the midgut setting that scored 9.

The authors state plainly that selection and sequencing of PRRT against everolimus, sunitinib, capecitabine/temozolomide and liver-directed therapy are not evidence-based and must rest on cross-trial comparison.
Evidence in grade 3 disease is explicitly described as limited, resting on a single series whose outcomes collapse above Ki-67 55%.
The effect of prior liver-directed therapy on PRRT hepatotoxicity, and the value of debulking before PRRT, are both acknowledged to rest on limited retrospective data.
critique: The appropriateness scores have no stated method behind them. The 1 to 9 scale is borrowed from appropriate-use-criteria methodology without the apparatus: no voting rounds, no panel size per scenario, no median or dispersion, no definition of agreement or disagreement, and no indication of whether scores were reached by discussion or by anonymous ballot. A score of 8 for pancreatic NET is therefore an assertion in the form of a number.

The PRISMA review that supports the document is reported as a count. One thousand one hundred and ninety-five articles screened and 153 included, with no risk-of-bias assessment, no evidence tables and no grading, so a single randomised trial and a run of retrospective series feed the same scores on the same footing.

The document contradicts itself on a score it is meant to deliver: use of 177Lu-DOTATATE in place of 131I-iobenguane in MIBG-positive paraganglioma is scored 6 in the text and 5 in Table 1, which straddles the boundary between may be appropriate and rarely appropriate.

The survival claim quoted for midgut disease has since been overturned. The preliminary overall survival hazard ratio of 0.4 with P=0.004 cited here fell far short of NETTER-1's own prespecified interim boundary, and the final analysis published in 2021 found no significant survival difference (HR 0.84, p=0.30). The score of 9 rests on progression-free survival alone.

The renal eligibility is widened substantially with little supporting data. Removing GFR under 50 as a contraindication, allowing GFR under 30 in exceptional circumstances and permitting treatment of dialysis patients with dose reduction and dosimetry are consequential statements, and no renal outcome series is cited for the dialysis recommendation.

The two statements that bear directly on surgical decisions point in opposite directions and each rests on one retrospective series: debulking before PRRT may improve response and progression-free survival, while prior liver-directed therapy may raise PRRT hepatotoxicity. A surgeon is left to weigh two single-series observations against each other.

The choice between PRRT and hepatic arterial embolisation in liver-dominant disease is handed over as a cross-trial comparison between an approximately 50% radiographic response rate from embolisation meta-analyses and the 18% response rate in NETTER-1, measured by different criteria in different populations with different endpoints.

Scenarios are scored by primary site and not by hepatic tumour burden, although the document's own reference list includes a NETTER-1 analysis of baseline liver tumour burden. For a patient whose problem is the liver, the appropriateness framework has no axis.
No ceiling is set for grade 3 disease, although the series the document cites shows median progression-free survival falling to 4 months and overall survival to 7 months above Ki-67 55%.

No funding statement and no conflict-of-interest declaration appears anywhere in the document, which is a joint society statement on the appropriate use of a single commercial product whose authors include many of the investigators on that product's registration trial.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so the appropriateness scores entered practice without published external appraisal.
32015164.n: No patient cohort. A 14-member multidisciplinary NANETS/SNMMI workgroup, including one patient advocate, scored clinical scenarios for appropriateness, informed by a PRISMA literature review that screened 1195 articles and included 153.
32015164.bottom_line: This is the document that defines who should receive 177Lu-DOTATATE in North America: somatostatin receptor uptake exceeding liver as an absolute prerequisite, a score of 9 for midgut NET progressing on a somatostatin analogue, 8 for pancreatic and unknown primaries, 7 and 6 for bronchial carcinoid, and a substantial relaxation of the renal threshold. Only one randomised trial sits behind it, and the survival figure it quotes for that trial, a preliminary hazard ratio of 0.4, was later shown to be non-significant. The scores themselves come from an expert workgroup with no stated voting method, agreement statistic or evidence grading, the sequencing of PRRT against everolimus, chemotherapy and liver-directed therapy is conceded to be non-evidence-based, and the two statements that most affect a surgeon, that debulking before PRRT may help and that prior liver-directed therapy may raise hepatotoxicity, each rest on a single retrospective series.

limitations: The approximately 85% five-year survival after curative resection of liver metastases is attributed by the panel partly to preselection bias.
Liver metastases are often more extensive than appreciated even at operation, which the guideline states directly.
The role of debulking in non-functioning GEP-NET is called unclear, and no cytoreduction target is offered anywhere in the document.

The guideline records a dissenting position from one of its own authors, E. P. Krenning, who holds that PRRT should come earlier in SSTR-positive pancreatic NET and should rank equal to everolimus in small intestinal NET G2 with Ki-67 above 10%.
PRRT toxicity is stated plainly: up to 3% to 4% of patients develop irreversible marrow toxicity and about 30% long-term grade 1 or 2 renal toxicity.
Nearly all surgical and locoregional recommendations carry levels of evidence IV to V and grades B to C, the weakest categories the guideline uses.
critique: The most common operative question in neuroendocrine liver metastasis is left unanswered. No cytoreduction target of any kind is given, so a surgeon consulting the principal European guideline finds debulking endorsed for symptom relief in functioning disease, called unclear in non-functioning disease, and attached to no threshold.

A Ki-67 of 10% recurs as the operative boundary for first-line somatostatin analogues, for debulking and for transplantation, without any analysis supporting 10% rather than any neighbouring value. It is a convention used as a threshold in three separate decisions.

The transplant criteria, which are the most specific operative statement in the document, appear in figure footnotes rather than in graded recommendation text, and they are stricter than the criteria of the series that generated them: the Milan cohort treated age under 60 as a relative criterion and included patients whose liver involvement exceeded 50% and whose grade was later revised to G3.

Grade A is attached to level IV evidence more than once. Using locoregional therapy early after a somatostatin analogue in functional NET to prevent carcinoid crisis is [IV, A], and watch-and-wait at Ki-67 under 2% is [IV, A]: the strongest recommendation grade on evidence the same guideline classifies as among its weakest, with no trial behind either.

The statement that locoregional therapy may be used instead of resecting resectable liver metastases is graded [V, C], the weakest combination in the document, and directly contradicts the surgical pathway set out a few paragraphs earlier. No comparative data are cited.

The comparative material a liver surgeon needs, on chemoembolisation against bland embolisation against radioembolisation against ablation, is deferred to supplementary material and is not graded in the main text, so the guideline offers no graded basis for choosing between techniques.

The recommendation against upfront surgery in high-grade disease and in extra-abdominal metastasis is [IV, B], while the absolute bar in advanced NEC G3 is [IV, A], so the same evidence level supports a cautionary recommendation and an absolute contraindication.

PRRT is placed after all approved therapies in pancreatic NET [III, A] while an author of the guideline dissents in favour of earlier use. That author declares an employment interest at Cyclotron Rotterdam BV together with stock or other interest, patent or intellectual property interest and travel from Advanced Accelerator Applications, which is the context in which the dissent is printed without resolution.

The guideline was finalised in March 2020, so its Ki-67 10% ceiling for first-line somatostatin analogue and its second-line placement of PRRT both predate the first-line radioligand evidence in grade 2 and grade 3 disease, and NETTER-2 appears only as a recently initiated trial.

Watch-and-wait at Ki-67 under 2% is endorsed at grade A without specifying an imaging interval or a duration beyond which it stops being safe, in a disease where the comparator trials show untreated median times to progression of between 6 and 18 months.

Most authors declare honoraria, advisory roles or research funding from Novartis, Ipsen, Advanced Accelerator Applications, Pfizer and Lexicon, the manufacturers of the somatostatin analogues and radioligand therapy the guideline positions.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
32272208.bottom_line: This is the principal European guideline for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms and it sets the boundaries a liver surgeon works within: surgery for selected stage IV disease with liver-predominant involvement, debulking for hormonal symptoms but generally not above Ki-67 10%, transplantation only under six simultaneous criteria, and PRRT second line in midgut NET but last in pancreatic NET. It gives no cytoreduction threshold at all, calls the role of debulking in non-functioning disease unclear, and grades almost every surgical and locoregional statement at level IV to V, conceding that the 85% five-year survival after curative resection partly reflects preselection. It also predates the first-line radioligand data, and it prints an unresolved dissent on PRRT sequencing from an author with declared employment, stock and intellectual-property interests in that field.
32272208.funding: No external funding was received for the preparation of these guidelines; production costs were covered by ESMO from central funds. Disclosures: M. Pavel reports advisory and presentation honoraria from Novartis, Ipsen, Pfizer, Advanced Accelerator Applications and Lexicon and research funding from Ipsen and Novartis; M.F. reports presentation honoraria from Novartis, Ipsen, Advanced Accelerator Applications and Prime Oncology, advisory honoraria from Advanced Accelerator Applications and research funding from Ipsen and Novartis; E. P. Krenning declares an employment interest at Cyclotron Rotterdam BV and stock or other interest, patent or intellectual property interest, travel, accommodation and expenses from Advanced Accelerator Applications; A.S. reports lecture honoraria from Ipsen and honoraria from Advanced Accelerator Applications; A.B. reports consultancy, advisory and speaking fees from Bayer, Janssen, Astellas and Novartis with research grants from Janssen and Astellas; A.P. and K. Oberg declare none.

limitations: The panel names its own consensus threshold as a limitation: in multiple-option questions only 50% preferring one answer was required, so several reported statements rest on 54 to 58% agreement.

Consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions, several of them management-deciding, and the panel tabulates them: second-line therapy for non-resectable pancreatic NET (PRRT reached only 65 to 70%), the right point in the sequence for PRRT, PRRT for local non-resectable disease, PRRT with mismatched lesions, and neoadjuvant PRRT.

The panel declined to recommend PRRT as second line in pancreatic NET because no study compares PRRT with sunitinib, everolimus or streptozocin-based chemotherapy, so the headline second-line statement applies to gastrointestinal primaries only.
The criteria defining the disease stability that licenses PRRT rechallenge are acknowledged to be unstandardised, with trials lacking.
Extension of PRRT to G3 NET rests on two small retrospective series restricted to Ki-67 under 55%.

Panellists were drawn from high-volume centres with full access to Ga-68-DOTA-SSA PET/CT and PRRT, while a 2017 survey of 443 respondents in 26 countries found both perceived as limited, and 56 of 60 ENETS centres of excellence are in Europe.

The panel stresses that RECIST size criteria capture slow-growing NET poorly, and that PET/CT can miss small liver lesions against high background which arterial-phase or hepatocyte-specific MRI detects better.

The document records that its recommendations conflict with other guidance: it rejects F-18-DOPA for small intestine NET although EANM guidelines list it as an additional first choice, and on monitoring EANM favours Ga-68-DOTA-SSA, ESMO favours CT and NCCN recommends SSTR imaging only at 12 to 36 months, while this panel reached no consensus at all.
critique: Every company whose product the consensus recommends paid for the meeting. The EANM Focus 3 meeting was supported by unrestricted grants from Advanced Accelerator Applications (Novartis), which markets Lu-177-DOTATATE, ITM, which supplies the radioisotope, Ipsen, which markets lanreotide, and Siemens Healthineers, which makes PET scanners. The declaration of interests then records fees, grants or advisory roles with those same companies for almost every panellist.

The assurance that sponsors had no direct or indirect influence is an assertion, not a procedure. No recusal rule, no independent non-conflicted chair, no conflict-weighted voting and no blinded vote collection is described anywhere in the methods.

The panel's composition is weighted toward the speciality that provides the tests. Nine of 24 members are nuclear medicine physicians against one surgeon, one pathologist, one gastroenterologist and two radiologists, and the panel voted that Ga-68-DOTA-SSA PET/CT is necessary at staging in all NET, at restaging after both curative and non-curative surgery, and before PRRT.

The evidence base is thinner than the output. Twenty-two qualifying studies across five topics is about four per topic, no risk-of-bias appraisal or GRADE rating is attached to any statement, and the document makes 31 recommendations from that base.

The percentages are not comparable with one another. Denominators move between 20 and 24 question by question because panellists could abstain or declare themselves unqualified, so 95.2% is 20 of 21 and 70.0% is 14 of 20, and no overall agreement statistic for the exercise is reported.

The literature search closed on 16 March 2019 and the meeting was held in February 2020, so NETTER-1's final overall survival analysis, published in 2021 and showing no significant survival benefit, could not inform any PRRT recommendation here. The PRRT statements rest on the positive progression-free survival report alone.

Allowing progression to be declared on new lesions at SSTR imaging with a stable CT changes who gets treated and when, and the criterion is adopted without validation against any outcome, in the same document that reached no consensus on monitoring interval or modality.

Two of the dosimetry statements pull against each other and both sit near the consensus floor: dosimetry belongs in clinical trials (12 of 21, 57.1%) while administered activity should be adapted to dosimetry or to patient factors (14 of 21, 66.7%).

Making Ga-68-DOTA-SSA PET/CT necessary at staging and restaging in all NET has resource consequences the document never addresses. No cost, capacity or access analysis accompanies the recommendation, in a paper that itself cites survey evidence of limited availability.
One of the 24 panellists is a patient advocate and no patient-reported outcome, quality-of-life or cost consideration appears in any of the 31 recommendations.
Medical writing was provided by a commercial medical writing firm and project management by the sponsoring society's own staff, in a document whose authority rests on being an independent consensus.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so this consensus entered the literature without published external appraisal.
33588146.n: No patient cohort. A 24-member multidisciplinary panel voted on 43 questions over a modified three-round Delphi process, built on a systematic PubMed review to 16 March 2019 that identified 22 qualifying studies across five topics; denominators per question range from 20 to 24 because panellists could abstain or declare themselves unqualified.
33588146.bottom_line: This is the document that fixed current practice in somatostatin receptor imaging and PRRT selection: Ga-68-DOTA-SSA PET/CT as the preferred technique and as necessary alongside CT or MRI at staging and restaging, FDG PET to find the mismatched lesion, and PRRT as second line after a somatostatin analogue in gastrointestinal NET with Krenning 3 to 4 uptake in all metastases. What it does not settle is almost everything a tumour board argues about: consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions including second-line therapy in pancreatic NET, the point in the sequence at which PRRT belongs, PRRT with mismatched lesions and neoadjuvant PRRT. The recommendations rest on 22 qualifying studies with no quality grading, several pass at 50 to 58% agreement, the search predates NETTER-1's negative survival analysis, and the meeting was funded by the manufacturers of the drugs and scanners being recommended.
33588146.funding: The EANM Focus 3 meeting was funded by the EANM and supported by unrestricted grants from Advanced Accelerator Applications (a Novartis company), ITM Isotopen Technologien Munchen AG, Ipsen and Siemens Healthineers; the paper states these sponsors had no direct or indirect influence on the programme, content or writing. Medical writing services were provided by Bean Medical Writing. Almost every panellist declares personal fees, grants or advisory roles with Advanced Accelerator Applications/Novartis, Ipsen, ITM, Bayer, Telix, Curium, Siemens Healthineers or related companies, and one declares participation in the NETTER-1 and COMPETE trials.

limitations: During long-term follow-up 36% of control patients received PRRT as subsequent treatment, most of them early (23% by 24 months after randomisation), which the authors name as a limitation of the analysis.
The rank-preserving structural failure time adjustment for that crossover assumes a constant treatment effect regardless of when PRRT was received.
Other confounding factors clearly existed: 24% of patients received further antineoplastic agents.
More than 35% of patients in each group survived 5 years regardless of their assigned treatment, so a large subpopulation had extended survival independent of the intervention.
20% of patients were censored because of consent withdrawal or loss to follow-up.

The proportional-hazards assumption required by the Cox analysis of overall survival was not fulfilled (Schoenfeld residuals test p = 0.03), which is why a restricted mean survival time analysis was performed.

Long-term survival analysis in an indolent tumour type is acknowledged to be difficult because of extended survival, the potential for crossover and the availability of subsequent therapies; the authors note phase 3 somatostatin analogue trials in similar populations also failed to show an overall survival benefit despite large progression-free survival gains.

During long-term follow-up the protocol required reporting only of serious adverse events deemed related to 177Lu-Dotatate and of adverse events of special interest in the 177Lu-Dotatate group, and did not require reporting of all adverse events in both groups.
critique: This analysis is negative on its own prespecified terms and is written as though it were not. The final significance threshold after alpha spending was 0.049915, the observed two-sided p value was 0.30 and the hazard ratio was 0.84 with a confidence interval from 0.60 to 1.17. Describing the 11.7-month median difference as clinically relevant is an argument about a result the trial failed to demonstrate.

The trial never reached the event count it was powered for. Eighty per cent power required 158 deaths; the 5-year calendar cutoff arrived first with 142, so the definitive survival question was answered with less evidence than the protocol said it needed.

By the last timepoint the two arms had the same number of deaths: 65 of 117 (56%) with 177Lu-Dotatate and 63 of 114 (55%) in the control arm. The entire restricted mean survival time advantage accrues in years 2 to 4 and its 5-year difference of 5.1 months has a confidence interval from -0.5 to 10.7 that includes zero.

Both analyses that carry the positive reading were added late. The restricted mean survival time analysis and the rank-preserving structural failure time crossover adjustment were specified in a statistical analysis plan amendment before final data cutoff and conditional on the proportional-hazards assumption failing, which it then did.

The crossover adjustment rests on an assumption the authors themselves flag as untenable, a treatment effect constant in time, when 23% of controls crossed over within the first 24 months. Even so, the adjusted hazard ratio of 0.73 has a confidence interval of 0.40 to 1.34 and does not exclude no effect.

The long-term safety comparison is structurally one-sided. By protocol, only the 177Lu-Dotatate arm had to report treatment-related serious adverse events and events of special interest during long-term follow-up, so the 2% myelodysplastic syndrome rate has no control denominator and the claim that no new safety signals emerged describes a collection designed to look at one arm.

One fifth of the cohort was censored for consent withdrawal or loss to follow-up in a survival analysis, and no sensitivity analysis for informative censoring is presented. Patients who withdraw after progression are not a random sample.

The Karnofsky 60-80 subgroup hazard ratio of 0.45 (95% CI 0.26-0.78) is one of roughly twenty prespecified subgroup analyses, spanning stratification factors, four age cuts, sex, three body-mass-index bands, region, race, OctreoScan grade and burden, performance status, prior therapies, tumour grade and two baseline markers. No multiplicity adjustment and no interaction test is reported, and the control arm's median survival in that subgroup was under a year.

The registrational primary endpoint was recomputed after publication. The progression-free survival hazard ratio is given here as 0.18 (0.11-0.29) against the published 0.21 (0.13-0.33), following health-authority re-review of baseline scans, and the randomised denominators are 117 and 114 here against 116 and 113 in the primary report because two patients randomised after the enrolment cutoff are now included.

Creatinine clearance fell by a similar amount in both arms over 5 years, by 21.6 mL/min with 177Lu-Dotatate and 24.7 mL/min on octreotide. That is genuinely reassuring about radioligand nephrotoxicity and it also means the renal decline observed here is not attributable to treatment in either direction, a point the renal safety paragraph does not make.

A diffuse large B-cell lymphoma occurring during long-term follow-up is reported separately from the myelodysplastic syndrome count, so the secondary haematological malignancy burden is higher than the headline figure of 2% conveys.

The comparator and the selection method are both obsolete. The control arm is octreotide LAR 60 mg, a dose with no antitumour pedigree, and eligibility required uptake on 111In-DTPA-octreotide scintigraphy rather than 68Ga- or 64Cu-DOTATATE PET, which identifies a different and larger population today.

The sponsor ran the analysis. Advanced Accelerator Applications, a Novartis company, sponsored the trial, designed it through its own representatives with two named investigators, and analysed the data before providing them to the authors for interpretation. Two co-authors are Novartis employees, and the declaration of interests records consulting, speakers bureau and research funding from the sponsor or Novartis for most of the senior authors.

A linked comment accompanies this paper (Virgolini, Lancet Oncol 2021;22:1645-6, PMID 34793720, titled as an important milestone). Its text was not accessible, so no position is attributed to it here.
34793718.n: 231 patients randomised at 41 sites in Europe and the USA between September 2012 and January 2016, 117 to 177Lu-Dotatate and 114 to high-dose octreotide; the final overall survival analysis was performed at 142 deaths, the 5-year calendar cutoff having arrived before the planned 158 deaths.
34793718.bottom_line: This is the analysis that settles what NETTER-1 did and did not show: 177Lu-Dotatate did not significantly improve overall survival, with medians of 48.0 against 36.3 months, a hazard ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.60-1.17) and p=0.30, and by five years the two arms had 65 and 63 deaths. No survival claim should be made from NETTER-1, and the positive framing rests on a restricted mean survival analysis and a crossover adjustment both added by late amendment, neither of which excludes no effect at five years. Its solid contribution is long-term safety: no new signals after 2016, myelodysplastic syndrome in 2% including one death, and a five-year fall in creatinine clearance no greater than in the control arm, though during long-term follow-up only the treated arm was required to report adverse events at all.
