Two co-authors are Novartis employees. The declaration of interests records consulting, advisory, speakers bureau and research-funding relationships with Advanced Accelerator Applications and Novartis for the senior authors, alongside Ipsen, Lexicon, Sirtex Medical, ITM and Xencor.

limitations: The two cohorts were not perfectly balanced at baseline: the transplant group was younger, had higher Ki-67 at pathology and a higher rate of nodal involvement of the primary tumour.
There may be a selection bias toward young patients, who because of longer life expectancy are offered transplantation more often despite adverse prognostic factors.

The interval from resection of the primary to liver surgery was significantly longer in the transplant group, adding a test of time that screens out rapidly progressive disease; whether this selected more favourable biology is difficult to assess.
The study is a single-centre experience spanning more than three decades, during which indications, classifications and organ-allocation policies all changed and influenced the results.
No intention-to-treat analysis accounting for drop-out from the transplant waiting list could be performed.
The two groups were retrospectively selected from historical cohorts and selection bias cannot be excluded; the cohort of a little over a hundred patients is relatively small.
The authors state the retrospective design prevents practice-changing conclusions because of the high risk of selection bias, and that all conclusions need confirmation.

Transplantation requires lifelong immunosuppression predisposing to infection, de novo tumours and cardiovascular disease, which the series shows directly: 6 of the 9 deaths after transplantation were not cancer related but likely due to transplant sequelae.
Liver resection is conceded to be a suboptimal locoregional treatment because tumour is almost always left behind whatever the type of resection.

Whether the predominance of lymphatic recurrence after transplantation reflects indirect selection of a different tumour biology by the Milan criteria is left open; nodal status of the primary is not part of those criteria.
critique: The two arms were defined by resectability, not allocated. Resection was offered to resectable disease and transplantation only when R0 was technically impossible or the remnant would be insufficient, so meeting the Milan criteria equalises tumour burden while leaving the arms differing on the one feature that determined treatment. The conclusion that clinicians should consider upfront transplantation in resectable patients applies to a group that was never transplanted here.

Nothing is adjusted. Table 4 is headed 'univariate analysis of factors independently associated with OS and DFS', a contradiction in terms, and contains a single row, liver transplantation. No multivariable model exists, so the 93% versus 75% difference is unadjusted for age, Ki-67, liver involvement, nodal status or era, all of which differ between arms.

The univariate table reports only the factor that was positive. Which other candidate variables were tested, and how many, is never shown, so the reader cannot judge the selection or the multiplicity.

The nodal-involvement results inside the transplant group are internally impossible as printed. Disease-free survival is given as HR 2.6 (95% CI 1.1-5.9) with p=.22, a p value incompatible with a confidence interval that excludes 1, and overall survival as HR 5.7 (95% CI 1.3-24) with p=.004, which is also far smaller than that interval width implies.

Table 2 contradicts the eligibility flow. All 48 transplanted patients are said to meet the Milan criteria, yet 7 of them (15%) have liver involvement above 50% and 2 (4%) are G3, while the flow text says H3 and G3 patients were the ones excluded. Either the criteria were applied inconsistently or the table is wrong, and the central claim of the paper depends on which.

The resection arm was given a lesser operation on the variable that matters most. No routine lymphadenectomy was performed for resection, while every transplant included hilar clearance of stations 12b, 12p, 12a, 8 and 9, and 33% of transplanted patients had positive hilar nodes. Nodal involvement is then reported as the only predictor of post-transplant outcome, from a staging procedure only one arm received.
Six of 56 resections (11%) were R1 and are counted inside a cohort defined as surgery with curative intent.

Survival is measured from liver surgery, and the transplant group reached that point a median of 38.5 months after resection of the primary against 6.5 months for the resection group. Transplanted patients therefore had to survive roughly three extra years of observed metastatic disease to enter the analysis, and unlike the same group's 2016 paper no left truncation or landmark is applied.

The primary endpoint is the one that flatters transplantation most. Only 3 of 9 deaths after transplantation were cancer related against 17 of 19 after resection, so overall survival mixes cancer deaths with immunosuppression deaths in opposite proportions. A cancer-related survival curve is plotted in Figure 2C and no cancer-specific rate, hazard ratio or p value is given anywhere in the text or tables.

Disease-free survival compares an organ that was removed with an organ that was not. Eighty-eight per cent of resection recurrences were hepatic and 8% of transplant recurrences were, so most of the 52% versus 18% gap at 10 years is a statement about which organ remained at risk rather than about disease control.

Post-recurrence survival did not differ between the arms (p=.276, 5-year 72% versus 69%), which argues that once disease returns the two strategies converge. The paper reports the figure and does not weigh it against its conclusion.

No perioperative harm is reported for either operation: no 90-day mortality, no complication rate, no graft loss or retransplantation figure, in a paper whose own definition of unresectability turns on a predicted perioperative mortality above 3% and whose discussion invokes the technical complexity and morbidity of transplantation.

The discussion states that donors of marginal or poor quality were used in the large majority of these transplants, and the paper reports no donor age, steatosis, cold ischaemia or donor risk index at all.

The claim that the transplant group had worse biology, which is the main defence against confounding, rests on incomplete and non-significant data. Primary nodal status is known in only 24 of 48 transplanted and 44 of 56 resected patients, so the 79% versus 18% N+ difference comes from half the transplant arm, while Ki-67 (median 3 versus 2, p=.061) and grading (p=.187) do not differ significantly even though the text asserts higher Ki-67 and more G2-G3 tumours.

The supporting subgroup analysis adds 33 resection patients over 60 and no transplant patients (48 versus 89), so it compares the same transplant cohort with an older resection cohort and is then presented as confirming the result.

Thirty-six years of accrual are never analysed by era, although Figure 1 shows the distribution over time and the authors list changing indications, classifications and allocation policy among their limitations. Immunosuppression, Ga-68 PET staging, somatostatin analogues and the WHO grading system all changed inside the study window.

The Milan-in proportion differs sharply between arms, 91% of transplants against 58% of resections, chiefly because 37 resection patients were older than 60. Age thus both filters the resection arm and separates the two groups, and it is the variable the authors concede drives transplant selection.

The benchmark the paper measures itself against is its own. The 2016 Milan analysis is cited as 'the only available prospective study on this topic' when that paper describes itself as a retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected cohort, and roughly half the reference list is the same group's work. A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment on this paper.
35869798.n: 104 of 149 patients (70%) operated with curative intent for liver-only neuroendocrine liver metastases at one centre between 1984 and 2019 whose burden met the Milan criteria: 48 of 53 transplanted and 56 of 96 resected.
35869798.bottom_line: Within one centre's Milan-in population, transplantation was followed by 93% ten-year survival and 52% ten-year disease-free survival against 75% and 18% after resection, with recurrence after resection almost always hepatic and after transplantation almost always nodal or multisite. It does not show that transplantation is the better operation for a given patient, because the two arms were separated by resectability itself, nothing is adjusted beyond a single-row univariate table, survival is timed from an operation the transplant group reached three years later, and the primary endpoint counts 6 deaths from transplant sequelae alongside 17 cancer deaths in the resection arm. Post-recurrence survival was identical in the two groups (p=.276), and the paper's own conclusion that resectable patients should be offered upfront transplantation describes a population it never transplanted.
35869798.funding: No specific funding was assigned to the project; open access funding provided by BIBLIOSAN. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

limitations: The absence of a non-temozolomide control arm precludes any definitive conclusion about whether MGMT deficiency is predictive rather than merely associated with response.

MGMT promoter methylation does not fully explain MGMT downregulation, since many more patients had low expression by immunohistochemistry, and the authors state there is insufficient evidence to support routine MGMT testing in metastatic pancreatic NET.
The absence of an overall survival benefit is attributed to relatively long survival, the effect of poststudy treatments and lack of statistical power to detect a difference.
Time from diagnosis was longer in the combination arm (34.3 versus 25.5 months), which the authors say could have dampened the efficacy result in that arm.

Second primary cancers in 4% and 5% may reflect the long median follow-up of 59.9 months and the known association of neuroendocrine tumours with second primaries; the authors call for better characterisation of these toxicities in future studies.
177Lu-DOTATATE has never been evaluated in a randomised trial in pancreatic NET, so no accurate comparison of progression-free survival with that option is possible.
The subgroup who had MGMT testing differed from the study population by sex, with a female predominance among those tested by promoter methylation against a male predominance overall.
critique: The trial was declared positive against an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 at 76% information time, a threshold no phase III trial would accept, and the effect then attenuated: the final hazard ratio was 0.71 with a confidence interval of 0.46 to 1.07, and the grade-adjusted figure 0.63 (0.39-1.01). Both cross 1.

The numbers in general circulation are the interim ones. The abstract conclusion and most citations use 22.7 against 14.4 months with HR 0.58, the values from the analysis that triggered the stop, rather than the final 23.2 against 15.1 months with a non-significant hazard ratio.

The response-rate advantage the combination is credited with does not exist in this trial: 39.7% against 33.8%, P=0.59. The discussion nonetheless sets its 39.7% against lanreotide at 2%, everolimus at 5% and sunitinib at 9% to argue that temozolomide-based regimens stand apart, when the trial's own randomised comparison shows that single-agent temozolomide achieves the same thing. The response argument supports temozolomide, not the addition of capecitabine.

An apparently large interim survival benefit evaporated. At interim, median overall survival was 38 months against not reached, HR 0.41, P=0.012; at final analysis it was 53.8 against 58.7 months, HR 0.82, P=0.42. A trial that stopped accrual on the strength of its interim data produced two interim signals, both of which shrank.
The explanation offered for the survival null cannot be examined, because poststudy treatment data were not collected at all. Subsequent therapy is invoked as the reason and no record of it exists.

Eleven of 144 randomised patients were excluded from the analysed population, three of them after central pathology review, so the eligible population of 133 is defined partly by assessments made after randomisation.

Entry required radiographic progression within 12 months and the paper states that progression was not defined by RECIST 1.1, so the eligibility criterion that makes this a trial in progressive disease rested on local judgement.

Central pathology review found more grade 2 tumours in the temozolomide arm, and time from diagnosis differed by nine months between arms. In a 133-patient trial these imbalances are the size of the effect being measured, and the only adjustment offered is the grade-adjusted hazard ratio, which is also non-significant.

The MGMT methylation result rests on seven patients. An odds ratio of 9.79 with a confidence interval from 1.09 to 87.71 spans nearly two orders of magnitude, the methylation subgroup was tested in 57 of 133 patients, the immunohistochemistry subgroup in 97, and the tested patients differed from the trial population by sex.

Because both arms received temozolomide, the MGMT finding cannot distinguish a predictive biomarker from a prognostic marker of temozolomide sensitivity. The authors say so plainly, and the result is nonetheless routinely cited as predictive.

Over 92% of patients had liver metastases and the paper reports no hepatic tumour burden, no liver-specific endpoint and no analysis by extent of liver involvement, so nothing here helps in choosing between this regimen and a liver-directed option.
Both arms were capped at 13 cycles, so the regimen tested is a fixed 13-cycle course and the trial says nothing about treatment continued to progression, which is how the combination is often given.

A great deal now rests on this result. The authors propose capecitabine and temozolomide as a standard option and as the comparator arm for future trials, and two NCTN studies have been built on it, an adjuvant trial (SWOG 2104) and a randomised comparison against 177Lu-DOTATATE (A022001), all descending from a phase II result declared at alpha 0.119 whose final hazard ratio includes no effect.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so this trial entered practice without independent published appraisal.
36260828.n: 144 patients with advanced progressive low- or intermediate-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours randomised 1:1 across ECOG-ACRIN sites from 2013 to 2016, of whom 133 were eligible for analysis (65 temozolomide, 68 capecitabine plus temozolomide); over 92% had liver metastases, and MGMT was assessed by immunohistochemistry in 97 and by promoter methylation in 57.
36260828.bottom_line: E2211 is the only randomised evidence for capecitabine plus temozolomide in advanced progressive pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, and at its interim analysis it met its primary endpoint with a median progression-free survival of 22.7 against 14.4 months. The threshold it met was an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119, and in the final analysis the hazard ratio was 0.71 (95% CI 0.46-1.07), overall survival was 53.8 against 58.7 months (P=0.42) and the response rate did not differ at all (39.7% against 33.8%, P=0.59) while grade 3-4 toxicity doubled. What it establishes is that temozolomide-based treatment produces response rates far above everolimus, sunitinib or a somatostatin analogue in this disease; what it does not establish is that adding capecitabine is responsible, or that any of this lengthens life.

limitations: The authors state throughout that prospective and randomised data are lacking, and that no randomised trial underpins either first- or second-line therapy.

Predictive and prognostic biomarkers remain an unmet need; no blood biomarker is established for routine use, and the prognostic markers described (chromogranin A, NSE, LDH, alkaline phosphatase, platelets) and the GI-NEC score are not prospectively validated.

Separating neuroendocrine carcinoma from well-differentiated NET G3 can be ambiguous, particularly for large-cell NEC, and the morphological distinction may be difficult even with immunohistochemistry.
Well-differentiated NET G3 is excluded from the guidance by design, because its prognosis, genetics and treatment differ.

The immunotherapy advice is hedged by the authors themselves: dual checkpoint inhibition is offered for later lines while they state that the vast majority of patients do not benefit and the data are insufficient for routine practice.

Most therapeutic recommendations carry the paper's weaker grades: surgery and chemoradiation for localised disease, adjuvant chemotherapy and first-line regimens at grade 4B, metastatic MiNEN and the advice against metastasectomy and PRRT at grade 5D.
critique: The statement that would end a liver resection discussion carries the weakest grade in the document. Surgery of metastatic disease and PRRT are 'generally not recommended' at grade 5D, that is expert opinion with the lowest strength, and no comparative data of any kind are cited against metastasectomy in selected patients with limited, resectable, chemotherapy-responsive hepatic NEC.

The Ki-67 55% cutoff that separates NEC from well-differentiated NET G3, and therefore decides which of two incompatible treatment pathways a patient enters, is drawn from a narrow evidence base while the authors concede that morphology is sometimes ambiguous. A patient at Ki-67 50% with poorly differentiated morphology and one at Ki-67 60% with well-differentiated morphology are routed in opposite directions on a threshold the paper does not defend quantitatively.

The two documents a tumour board uses together do not meet. This paper excludes NET G3 and the ENETS and ASCO NET guidance excludes NEC, so the Ki-67 20 to 55% poorly characterised patient falls between them, and that is exactly the patient about whom a surgical decision is hardest.

The survival figures that frame the whole document come from SEER, a registry with no central pathology review, in a disease whose definition changed across the period the registry covers. Median survival of 5.2 months for distant disease is therefore a mixture of true NEC and misclassified NET G3.

Palliative chemotherapy is credited with a median survival of 11 to 12 months against 1 month without, which is a comparison between treated patients and untreated patients in retrospective series, and the untreated figure describes people too unwell to be given chemotherapy. The guidance presents the contrast without qualification.

Performance status is reported as the dominant prognostic factor (18, 12 and 5 months at PS 0, 1 and 2) and is not integrated with any treatment recommendation, so the patients in whom chemotherapy is least likely to help are not identified as a group in whom it should be withheld.

Adjuvant platinum and etoposide after radical surgery is offered at grade 4B with no trial, no control arm and no estimate of absolute benefit, in a population whose 5-year survival after surgery is already stated as 25 to 40%.

First-line carboplatin and etoposide is recommended with a 30 to 50% response rate and a 4 to 6 month progression-free survival, which places the whole treatment pathway inside the span of a single imaging interval, and the guidance offers no stopping rule or re-assessment schedule.

The grading system is used in a way that obscures rather than clarifies. Grades 1A, 2aB, 2bB, 2bC, 3aB, 4A, 4B, 5A and 5D all appear, the tables defining them are supplementary and not in the text, and the strongest grade in the document (1A) is attached to a diagnostic definition while every therapeutic statement sits at 2b or weaker.

The conflict-of-interest statement is extensive: the lead author and most co-authors declare speaker or advisory honoraria from Novartis, Ipsen, Advanced Accelerator Applications, ITM, Bayer and others, with research grants from several, in a document whose recommendations include that somatostatin analogues must not be used and that PRRT is generally not indicated. The disclosures run against the recommendations here rather than with them, which is worth noting in both directions.
No funding statement appears anywhere, only an acknowledgement of the consensus meeting participants, so who paid for the working group's meeting is not stated.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment on this guidance.
36924180.n: No patient cohort. A multidisciplinary ENETS working group answered ten predefined questions from a MEDLINE search, with each recommendation graded, and circulated the draft to the participants of an ENETS Guidance Paper Consensus Meeting held on 13 October 2022.
36924180.bottom_line: This is the boundary document: for poorly differentiated digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma it keeps resection for localised disease, puts carboplatin and etoposide first line with a 4 to 6 month progression-free survival, and advises against both metastasectomy and PRRT, which is the opposite of the pathway used for well-differentiated NET. Almost nothing in it is prospective, the recommendation against operating on metastatic disease carries grade 5D, the weakest in the paper, and the prognostic figures come from a registry without central pathology review. Its sharpest practical limitation is deliberate: well-differentiated NET G3 is excluded, so the Ki-67 20 to 55% patient, the one for whom a liver-directed decision is genuinely contested, is addressed by neither this guidance nor its NET counterpart.

limitations: Almost every statement rests on level 3 to 5 evidence, that is case series and expert opinion, and the grades printed with the recommendations say so; no randomised data support any surgical or interventional recommendation in functioning pancreatic NET.

The timing and type of surgery for MEN1-related Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is explicitly called controversial and individualised, and the trade-off between about 30% cure of hypergastrinaemia at 5 years after duodenotomy and 60% to 80% at 10 years after pancreaticoduodenectomy is left to a conversation with the patient.
The diagnostic cutoffs for the rarer syndromes are conceded to be unvalidated.
The existence of a true somatostatinoma syndrome is questioned, and the WHO classification now reserves the term for symptomatic cases only.
The alternative route to a gastrinoma diagnosis, combining symptoms, a raised gastrin and a duodenopancreatic NET on imaging, carries the weakest grade in the scheme [5, D].
The paper addresses hormonal control rather than oncological treatment of pancreatic NET, which is deferred to a companion guidance paper.
critique: The cytoreduction target is written as a twenty-point range, 70% to 90% or more, with no guidance on which end applies to which patient. As printed it endorses the historic 90% convention and the newer 70% threshold simultaneously, which means it cannot be used to decide an operation.

Chemoembolisation is described as possibly more effective than bland embolisation on no comparative trial, in a disease where the only randomised comparison of embolotherapies closed one of its arms for severe complications rather than reporting efficacy.

The 40% response rate attributed to capecitabine and temozolomide comes from E2211, in which the combination's response rate did not differ from temozolomide alone (39.7% against 33.8%, P=0.59). Crediting that figure to the combination overstates what the trial showed.

PRRT's control of hypoglycaemia in 13 of 14 metastatic insulinomas is a fourteen-patient series carrying a recommendation, and the 9% hormonal flare rate is quoted without the denominator it came from.

Systematic peripancreatic lymphadenectomy for sporadic gastrinoma is given grade A on level 3 evidence, justified by a roughly 80% nodal metastasis rate even below 5 mm, with no data that clearing those nodes changes survival. A high prevalence of nodal disease is an argument for staging, not automatically for a bigger operation.

The grading is applied inconsistently. EUS-guided ablation for insulinoma carries level 2a with a weak grade C, while gastrinoma lymphadenectomy carries level 3 with the strongest grade A, so the letters and the numbers move independently of one another.

The enucleation criteria, a lesion under 2 to 3 cm and at least 3 mm from the main pancreatic duct, present a one-centimetre size band and a three-millimetre clearance as operative thresholds with no supporting measurement or outcome study.

Diagnosing gastrinoma requires measuring gastrin off proton pump inhibitors with a gastric pH of 2 or less, which exposes a patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome to acid-related complications during withdrawal. The requirement is stated at grade A without addressing that risk or specifying a safe withdrawal protocol.

The split between this document and the companion non-functioning pancreatic NET paper means a clinician treating a functioning pancreatic NET with liver metastases must combine two guidance papers that set different thresholds, and this one gives no Ki-67 limit for cytoreduction while ESMO sets 10%.
This European guidance is not harmonised with the NANETS surgical consensus statements, which address the same operations with different numbers and a different grading scheme.

No funding statement appears; the acknowledgements list only the participants of the consensus meeting. Most authors declare speaker or advisory fees from Ipsen, Novartis or Advanced Accelerator Applications, and one is a consultant to the interventional arm of a contrast-media manufacturer in a document that recommends transarterial therapy.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
37578384.n: No patient cohort. Nine clinical questions agreed at an ENETS Guidance Paper Consensus Meeting on 13 October 2022, each answered with a level of evidence (1a to 5) and a strength of recommendation (A to D).
37578384.bottom_line: This is the European reference for the functioning pancreatic NET syndromes, and its firm content is diagnostic and operative at the primary: gastrin above ten times normal with a gastric pH of 2 or less off acid suppression, a documented Whipple triad with a 72-hour fast for insulinoma, parenchyma-sparing resection without lymphadenectomy for insulinoma, and lymphadenectomy with duodenotomy for gastrinoma. For liver metastases it offers almost nothing usable: cytoreduction is endorsed at a target of 70% to 90% or more, a twenty-point range with no rule for choosing within it, and transarterial options are listed as equivalent alternatives with chemoembolisation called possibly better than bland on no comparative data. Every surgical and interventional statement carries level 2b to 5 evidence, and the MEN1 operation is explicitly left unresolved.

limitations: Almost every treatment recommendation is graded weak, which the panel defines as meaning that most informed people would choose the recommended course but a substantial number would not, and that appreciable uncertainty remains.

The panel states explicitly that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any particular sequence of therapies after progression, because the underlying trials used placebo controls with almost no head-to-head comparison.

Overall survival certainty was rated very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1, chiefly because of high crossover (85% in RADIANT-3, 69% in the sunitinib trial), so none of these agents has a demonstrated survival benefit.

The grade 3 recommendations rest on informal consensus and indirect evidence from grade 1 to 2 trials, rated very low quality, with five randomised trials (COMPETE, OCLURANDOM, NETTER-2, A022001 and COMPOSE) still pending at the time of writing.
No Ki-67 cut-off is supported within well-differentiated grade 3 disease.
There are no validated biomarkers; MGMT deficiency predicted response in E2211 but the panel judged it not ready for routine use.
Evidence supporting somatostatin analogues for tumour control is strongest at Ki-67 under 10%.
Surgery, liver-directed therapy and the control of hormonal syndromes were all placed outside the guideline's scope.
The systematic review excluded meeting abstracts not subsequently published, editorials, commentaries, letters, case reports, narrative reviews and all non-English publications.
critique: The review was restricted to phase III randomised trials, with phase II admitted only for chemotherapy, so 2,272 records collapsed to 11 publications from eight trials. Any question those eight trials did not address can only be answered by informal consensus, and the two recommendations a clinician meets first, multidisciplinary sequencing and baseline SSTR-PET in every patient, are informal consensus on low-quality evidence yet carry the guideline's strong recommendation grade.

The 70% to 90% cytoreduction threshold, the one number a liver surgeon would take away from an ASCO guideline, lies outside the guideline's own evidence process. Surgery and liver-directed therapy were excluded from the systematic review, so that figure and the mention of embolisation appear as ungraded narrative rather than as reviewed recommendations.

Recommending SSTR-PET with Ga-68-DOTA-peptides or Cu-64-DOTATATE in all patients has substantial cost and access consequences in exactly the community setting the guideline targets, and no resource or capacity consideration accompanies it. The advice against indium-111 pentetreotide comes from imaging commentary adapted from a staging manual rather than from the systematic review.

The evidence base is placebo-controlled throughout, which makes the question clinicians actually ask structurally unanswerable, and the guideline nonetheless prints a sequencing algorithm whose footnotes qualify nearly every arrow with 'uncertain', 'less common circumstance' or 'rare circumstance'.

Observation with imaging every 3 to 6 months is offered as an option in low-volume asymptomatic disease, which amounts to adopting CLARINET's placebo arm as a strategy. The guideline's own evidence tables print placebo time to progression as 6 months in PROMID and 18 months in CLARINET, a threefold discrepancy that is never reconciled even though it determines how safe watching actually is.

Harm is tabulated and then dropped. The evidence tables carry a relative risk of 9.91 for serious treatment-related adverse events in NETTER-1 and treatment-related myeloid neoplasia after PRRT of about 2.6%, and the PRRT recommendation itself contains no numerical statement of harm for a patient to weigh.

The quality and strength labels do not survive transmission. PRRT after somatostatin analogue failure is moderate quality with a weak recommendation, the whole grade 3 menu is very low quality with a weak recommendation, and both read in practice as endorsements of the listed drugs.

The conflict-of-interest paragraph states only that the majority of panel members disclosed no relationship constituting a conflict under ASCO policy, which concedes that a minority did. Individual disclosures are not printed in the article text, and no funding statement appears at all.

Excluding non-English publications and unpublished abstracts means trials reported only in abstract when the search closed, including NETTER-2 and OCLURANDOM, are absent from a guideline whose own limitations section identifies them as the trials that will change its conclusions.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so a guideline aimed explicitly at community oncologists entered the literature without published external appraisal.
37774329.n: No patient cohort. An ASCO Expert Panel including patient representatives worked from a PubMed search covering January 2005 to November 2022 and restricted to phase III randomised trials (phase II permitted for chemotherapy); 2,272 records were reduced to 11 publications from seven phase III and one phase II trial.
37774329.bottom_line: This is the systemic-therapy backbone for metastatic well-differentiated gastroenteropancreatic NET: somatostatin analogue first, PRRT after progression in receptor-positive gastrointestinal primaries, and an unordered menu of PRRT, capecitabine-temozolomide, everolimus and sunitinib for pancreatic primaries, with capecitabine-temozolomide favoured when the burden is high. It cannot answer the question it exists for, because the panel states plainly that no sequence can be recommended after progression and that overall survival certainty is very low for every agent except PRRT, where it is low, chiefly because of crossover. Almost every recommendation is graded weak, the grade 3 advice is informal consensus on very low quality evidence, and the 70% to 90% cytoreduction threshold a surgeon would take from it sits outside the systematic review altogether and should not be cited as this guideline's evidence.
37774329.funding: No funding statement appears in the article text. The Expert Panel was assembled under ASCO's Conflict of Interest Policy and all members completed ASCO's disclosure form; the paper states that, in accordance with that policy, the majority of panel members did not disclose any relationship constituting a conflict, with individual disclosures filed separately rather than printed.

limitations: The study was designed as open label because the two treatments are administered differently and radiation-exposure precautions are needed; bias was mitigated only through blinded central review of imaging.
Although open to patients aged 15 and over, no adolescents aged 15 to 17 were accrued, so the data relate to adults only.
Relative effectiveness against other available therapies, sequencing, cost-effectiveness and access all remain to be addressed in future research.
There is no defined standard of care and no robust data for this patient population, which is how the authors justify their choice of comparator.
Time to deterioration in quality of life did not differ between the groups, which the authors attribute to both arms receiving a somatostatin analogue backbone.
Overall survival data were immature, with the median not reached in either group, and 48% of control patients had crossed over to a radioligand after progression.
critique: The comparator was chosen for regulatory continuity rather than clinical relevance, and the paper's own defence of it is about tolerability, not activity: octreotide LAR 60 mg was selected by copying NETTER-1's FDA-guided design, and the justification offered is that the high dose had no notable side-effects and so is well tolerated. In grade 3 disease the retrospective PFS on a somatostatin analogue is cited at 4 to 8 months, and the control arm produced 8.5 months, so the trial beat the number it predicted.

The one comparison a tumour board needs is raised and then dropped. The discussion cites E2211's 40% response rate with capecitabine plus temozolomide in progressive pancreatic NET, numerically indistinguishable from this trial's own 43%, and no comparison with alkylating chemotherapy is made anywhere.

The population was not known to be progressing. Enrolment required diagnosis within the previous 6 months and excluded any documented progression, with short-course somatostatin analogue permitted only in the absence of progression. The control arm's 8.5-month median therefore measures the behaviour of untreated grade 2-3 disease in part, and the trial cannot say whether starting radioligand therapy at diagnosis is better than starting it at progression, which is the decision it is used to settle.

Somatostatin receptor uptake score 3 or 4 was required in every target lesion. Receptor heterogeneity rises with grade, so the trial enrolled the most uniformly receptor-avid slice of a grade 2-3 population and excluded the patients in whom the choice between PRRT and chemotherapy is hardest.

Any previous hepatic artery embolisation or radiofrequency ablation was an outright exclusion, and 90% of enrolled patients had liver metastases. The trial therefore excludes the neuroendocrine liver metastasis population that has already had liver-directed therapy, and it reports no analysis at all by hepatic tumour burden.

The grade range is narrower than the title suggests. Grade 3 was capped at Ki-67 55%, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma was excluded, the median Ki-67 across the whole cohort was 16% and 65% of patients were grade 2, so the cohort sits at the low end of the grades it claims to cover.

The 2:1 allocation leaves the control arm with 75 patients and 46 events, so the comparator median has a confidence interval from 7.7 to 13.8 months and every control subgroup contains a few dozen patients at most. The subgroup consistency the paper emphasises is consistency across very small denominators.

The experimental arm's median progression-free survival of 22.8 months is essentially equal to the median follow-up of 23.2 months, and its upper confidence limit is not estimable. The headline number sits at the edge of the observed data.

Tripling progression-free survival produced no detectable difference in how patients felt. Time to deterioration was no different for global health status, diarrhoea, fatigue or pain, and the paper reads this as encouraging rather than as a limit on what the primary endpoint means.
Crossover is built into the protocol, with patients still on crossover at the data cutoff, so the survival endpoint can never be clean in this trial and no future analysis will fix it.
Twelve per cent of treated patients did not receive all four cycles, and no analysis relates outcome to cycles received or to the median cumulative 29.2 GBq actually delivered.

First-line use spends the marrow early. Grade 3 or worse haematotoxicity occurred in 14% against 1%, one myelodysplastic syndrome had already appeared at about 14 months, and a median follow-up of 23.2 months cannot evaluate what moving a myelotoxic therapy to first line costs a patient who will need several more lines of treatment.

The conclusion claims first-line radioligand therapy as standard of care on the strength of progression-free survival and response rate alone, in the same paper that lists relative effectiveness, sequencing, cost-effectiveness and access as unanswered.

The sponsor designed the trial, sponsored it, and its own statistical team analysed the data before providing them to the authors, with a sponsor-funded medical writer assisting the manuscript. The declaration of interests runs to dozens of relationships, with the first author and most senior co-authors reporting Novartis support for this work alongside grants and consulting from the sponsor.

A linked Comment accompanies the paper (Ramirez and Eng, 'The developing role of theranostics in NETs', Lancet 2024;403:2759-61, PMID 38851204). Its full text was not obtained, so none of the points above draws on it.
38851203.n: 226 of 261 screened patients with newly diagnosed, inoperable, somatostatin-receptor-positive, well-differentiated higher grade 2 or grade 3 gastroenteropancreatic NET, randomised 2:1 at 45 centres in nine countries between January 2020 and October 2022: 151 to 177Lu-Dotatate plus octreotide LAR 30 mg and 75 to octreotide LAR 60 mg, of whom 147 and 73 were treated. Median Ki-67 was 16% and 90% had liver metastases.
38851203.bottom_line: NETTER-2 establishes that four cycles of 177Lu-Dotatate given first line in newly diagnosed, receptor-avid, well-differentiated grade 2-3 gastroenteropancreatic NET delays radiographic progression dramatically, from 8.5 to 22.8 months with a hazard ratio of 0.28, and produces a 43% response rate against 9%. It establishes nothing about survival, which is immature with 48% of controls crossed over, nothing about how patients feel, since time to quality-of-life deterioration was identical, and nothing about whether PRRT is better than the capecitabine-temozolomide it never tested. The enrolled population was newly diagnosed and not required to be progressing, needed uptake score 3 or 4 in every target lesion, and excluded anyone with prior hepatic embolisation or ablation, so a patient with heterogeneous uptake or previous liver-directed therapy is outside the evidence.
38851203.funding: Designed and sponsored by Advanced Accelerator Applications, a Novartis company, whose statistical team analysed the data and provided them to the authors for interpretation; a medical writer funded by the sponsor assisted with the manuscript. The declaration of interests records Novartis support for the present work and grants, consulting fees or meeting support from Novartis or Advanced Accelerator Applications for the first author and most senior co-authors, alongside extensive relationships with Ipsen, ITM, RayzeBio, Camurus, Telix, Curium and many others.

limitations: The surgical and locoregional recommendations carry the weakest grades in the document: B-4 for resecting liver metastases, B-3 for liver-directed therapy, and C-4 for operating on mesenteric fibrosis.
No high-quality data favour any one embolotherapy over another.
Recurrence after R0 resection of liver metastases is about 80% at 5 years, so lifelong follow-up is required and the operation is not curative.

Resection of the primary tumour in asymptomatic stage IV disease is explicitly unresolved: unmatched retrospective series favour resection, at least three propensity-matched studies show no survival benefit, and only 22% of a watch-and-wait cohort ever needed surgery.
Radioembolisation carries a risk of late liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.
HIPEC cannot currently be recommended for peritoneal disease.
Objective remissions with somatostatin analogues are rare, so first-line therapy is stabilisation only.
The randomised trial comparing bland embolisation, lipiodol chemoembolisation and drug-eluting-bead chemoembolisation closed its drug-eluting-bead arm because of increased severe complications.
Liver transplantation is described only as a rare consideration in selected individuals after resection of the primary leaves liver-only disease.
critique: Liver transplantation is reduced to a rare consideration without engaging the data that exist for it. The Milan-criteria literature reports 88.8% overall survival at 10 years in patients inside the same tumour-burden bracket this guidance describes, and no criteria, referral pathway or reason for the demotion is given.

No cytoreduction threshold appears anywhere, and no Ki-67 cut-off is set for operating on resectable liver metastases. The 70% versus 90% debulking question, which the North American guidance addresses however weakly, is not raised at all, so the two major guidance documents on this operation differ by omission rather than by argument.

The preference for bland embolisation is built from two pieces of evidence that do not test it. One retrospective study found no difference between chemoembolisation and radioembolisation, and a randomised trial closed its drug-eluting-bead arm on safety; neither compared bland embolisation with chemoembolisation, which is the comparison the recommendation makes.

Operating in high-volume centres is recommended on an observational 90-day mortality of 4% against 1%, with no definition of high volume given anywhere, so the recommendation cannot be acted on by a referring clinician.

A minimum of 8 lymph nodes is set as a standard with no evidence that the count changes outcome, and the companion North American pancreatic guidance sets 11 to 15 for a different primary site. Nodal yield in this disease is convention presented as a benchmark.

The survival figures that support resecting liver metastases, 71% to 74% at 5 years and 85% after R0, come from uncontrolled series of patients selected for resectability, as the same paragraph's 80% five-year recurrence rate makes plain.
The ablation criteria, at most 3 to 5 metastases each under 3 cm, present a range of ranges as an operative threshold with no derivation and no citation of a comparison across those numbers.

NETTER-2 is cited to support radioligand therapy in grade 2 and grade 3 disease, although that trial enrolled newly diagnosed patients with no documented progression, required uptake score 3 or 4 in every target lesion and excluded anyone with prior hepatic embolisation or ablation. That is precisely the population this guidance sends for liver-directed therapy, so the two recommendations do not describe the same patient.

Almost every member of the writing group declares honoraria, advisory fees or research funding from Ipsen, Advanced Accelerator Applications/Novartis or Pfizer, the makers of the first-line somatostatin analogues and the second-line radioligand, and one author is the inventor of and holds intellectual property rights on 64Cu-DOTATATE, a tracer the document endorses.
No funding statement appears anywhere in the paper.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment.
38977327.n: No patient cohort. An ENETS multidisciplinary writing group answered 10 key questions, with each recommendation given a strength (A to E) and an evidence level (1 to 5) under the scheme set out in the paper's appendix.
38977327.bottom_line: This is the current European reference for small intestine NET and its liver-metastasis content sits almost entirely in its weakest grades: resect liver-only G1/G2 disease if R0 is achievable (B-4), use liver-directed therapy in non-surgical candidates (B-3), prefer bland embolisation, keep ablation to at most three to five lesions under 3 cm, and treat the primary and mesenteric nodes aggressively in a high-volume centre. Its most useful admissions are negative: recurrence after R0 resection is about 80% at five years, no data favour one embolotherapy over another, and resection of the primary in asymptomatic stage IV disease is contradicted by three propensity-matched studies. It sets no cytoreduction threshold and no Ki-67 limit for liver surgery, and it reduces transplantation to a rare consideration without engaging the Milan-criteria outcomes for the same tumour burden.

limitations: The true incidence is unknown, partly because the criteria defining the diagnosis of carcinoid crisis are poor.

Octreotide prophylaxis is double-edged: octreotide within 48 hours, or octreotide LAR within 28 days, of 177Lu-Dotatate can competitively block tumour uptake and reduce the efficacy of the therapy, so the authors leave the trade-off to individual risk-benefit judgement.
There is no consensus on how many intravenous octreotide boluses should precede escalation to a continuous infusion.
Steroid prophylaxis is proposed but is not standard of care.
There is no consensus on whether PRRT should be re-attempted after a crisis, or on whether such patients are at higher risk of a further crisis.
The authors' own institution recorded no carcinoid crisis across 127 administrations in five years, so their experience does not corroborate the quoted incidence.
critique: The paper is a narrative review that calls itself a systematic one. No search dates, search strings, inclusion criteria, selection flow diagram, quality appraisal or PROSPERO registration appears anywhere, while the ethics statement describes the article as a systematic review.

The 1-2% incidence has no traceable denominator. It is quoted without a pooled count of events over treatments, in a condition the authors say lacks agreed diagnostic criteria, and the only cohort the paper contributes has zero events in 127 administrations, which is consistent with any true rate below roughly 2 to 3%.

The institutional audit cannot validate the review's own recognition framework. Ascertainment was retrospective, no definition was applied prospectively, and the single adverse event was attributed to bronchospasm rather than crisis by clinical reasoning alone, in a patient whose endobronchial carcinoid makes both explanations plausible.

The risk-factor list is assembled from case reports and small series with no multivariable analysis anywhere. Midgut primary, high tumour burden, liver metastases, raised 5-HIAA and chromogranin A, prior carcinoid syndrome, advanced age and concurrent beta-2 agonists are presented side by side as though each had been shown to act independently.

Debulking before PRRT is offered as a recognised preventive measure, which puts a surgeon in the prevention pathway, and no cited series shows that debulking reduces the incidence of crisis. The operative risk of debulking is nowhere weighed against an event rate of 1 to 2%.

The treatment regimen, 500 to 1000 micrograms of intravenous octreotide repeated every 5 minutes until control, carries no dose-finding evidence, no stated ceiling and no defined endpoint of control, for a condition the paper says has no agreed definition.

The two prophylaxis routes recommended are the same manoeuvres the review identifies as capable of blocking tumour uptake, and no threshold of risk is specified at which prophylaxis becomes worth the possible loss of therapeutic efficacy. The reader is told both that prophylaxis is advisable in patients with multiple risk factors and that it may undermine the treatment.

The reassurance that no deaths from this crisis had been reported as of May 2024 is a statement about the published case-report literature in a complication the paper itself describes as under-recognised and undefined.

Guidance elsewhere advises periprocedural intravenous somatostatin analogue for all patients with carcinoid syndrome regardless of long-acting analogue cover, which is more cautious than this review's risk-stratified approach, and the discrepancy is not reconciled.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so these recommendations stand unappraised.
39266864.n: No defined review cohort. The institutional component is an audit of 127 177Lu-Dotatate administrations at a single centre between October 2018 and February 2024, in which no carcinoid crisis occurred.
39266864.bottom_line: This is the only dedicated account of carcinoid crisis during 177Lu-Dotatate therapy and it is useful for exactly two things: the risk profile, in which midgut primary and high hepatic tumour burden dominate, and the recognition window, 12 to 48 hours after a dose, usually the first. Everything quantitative in it is weak: the 1 to 2% incidence has no pooled denominator in a condition the authors say has no diagnostic criteria, the paper is narrative despite describing itself as systematic, and the risk factors come from case reports with no multivariable analysis. For a surgeon the load-bearing claim is that pre-treatment debulking is a recognised preventive measure, and no series cited here shows that debulking reduces crisis incidence or that its operative risk is smaller than the event it prevents.
39266864.funding: None declared: the authors state that no funds, grants or other support were received during preparation of the manuscript, and that they have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

limitations: The trial was terminated early on the basis of interim analysis results, which the authors acknowledge could lead to overestimation of the treatment effect; they argue the progression-free survival analyses are relatively mature, with 111 of the planned 164 events in the extrapancreatic cohort and progression events in 57 of 95 pancreatic patients.

Placebo rather than an active comparator was used, which the authors justify on the grounds that no therapy has established efficacy after Lu-177 dotatate or targeted agents and that patients could have exhausted all available options before enrolment.

No overall survival difference has been observed, and the authors state the survival data were not mature and may have been affected by crossover and by the high rate of subsequent anticancer therapy.
A majority of patients treated with cabozantinib required dose modification or reduction to manage adverse events.
The authors state that the choice of therapy should be individualised and that future trials on the appropriate sequencing of therapy are needed.

They note that the phase 3 trials supporting everolimus, sunitinib and Lu-177 dotatate largely enrolled patients who had not yet received targeted therapy or radionuclide therapy, so those agents' results do not transfer to this later-line setting.
critique: The trial was stopped on a different endpoint from the one it reports. In May 2023 the data and safety monitoring board recommended that the protocol-specified interim progression-free survival analyses be performed on local assessments because the batched blinded central reads had fallen behind, and the recommendation to terminate followed from those local analyses. The primary endpoint presented is central review.

The alpha spent for efficacy at each interim was 0.001 one-sided, and the published analysis is the post-termination dataset with a data cutoff set to the date of unblinding and crossover. The reported hazard ratios are therefore the effect estimated at the moment the trial was judged positive, with 111 of 164 planned events in the larger cohort.

Follow-up is short relative to what is claimed. Median follow-up was 10.2 months in the extrapancreatic cohort against a cabozantinib median progression-free survival of 8.4 months, and 13.8 months in the pancreatic cohort against a median of 13.8 months. Both primary estimates sit at the edge of the observation window.

The comparator is placebo in a population with a median of two to three prior lines, so the trial establishes activity rather than comparative value. Cabozantinib has never been compared with capecitabine-temozolomide, with another VEGF-receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or with PRRT rechallenge, and the paper lists sequencing as an open question while presenting the drug as a new option.

In the extrapancreatic cohort the benefit is almost entirely the absence of progression rather than tumour shrinkage: a 5% confirmed response rate, all partial, against a placebo median progression-free survival of 3.9 months. What the trial mainly shows there is how fast untreated late-line extrapancreatic disease progresses.

Overall survival shows nothing in either cohort (hazard ratios 0.86 and 0.95), and the explanation offered, crossover in 33% and 41% plus subsequent therapy in 45% to 67%, is itself the reason no survival analysis of this trial will ever be interpretable.

Two thirds of patients could not take the assigned dose. Dose reduction was needed in 66% and 68%, bringing the median average daily dose to about 38 mg against the assigned 60 mg, so the regimen that produced these results is not the regimen that was randomised, and no dose-response or dose-intensity analysis is presented.

Discontinuation for adverse events reached 31% against 15% in the extrapancreatic cohort, and four patients in that arm had a grade 5 event judged at least possibly treatment-related, including two deaths of unspecified cause. For a drug whose benefit is measured in months of radiographic stability, those are the numbers that decide whether it is worth giving.

Quality of life stayed stable and similar between the groups, so a treatment that more than doubles progression-free survival produced no detectable difference in how patients felt, in a trial where two thirds needed dose reduction for toxicity.

Cohort allocation was imperfect in a trial whose two cohorts are analysed independently: 7 pancreatic patients were registered into the extrapancreatic cohort and 3 extrapancreatic patients into the pancreatic cohort, and the extrapancreatic cabozantinib arm had more unknown-primary tumours than placebo.

Grade 3 tumours were eligible and no result is broken down by grade, while poorly differentiated carcinoma was excluded, so the span from grade 1 to well-differentiated grade 3 is treated as one population in cohorts of 95 and 203.

The paper reports no hepatic tumour burden, no site-of-progression data and no liver-specific endpoint, so a trial in a population that is overwhelmingly liver-metastatic gives no information about how cabozantinib sits beside a liver-directed option.

Support came from the National Cancer Institute through Alliance and cooperative group awards and from Exelixis, which manufactures cabozantinib; individual disclosure forms were filed separately rather than printed.
An accompanying editorial was published with the paper (Rubin, Yeku and Morrissey, N Engl J Med 2024, PMID 39282952). Its text was not obtained, so no point above draws on it.
39282913.n: 298 patients in two independent cohorts at 62 US sites, enrolled October 2018 to August 2023: 203 with extrapancreatic and 95 with pancreatic well or moderately differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib or placebo within each cohort, all with progression in the previous 12 months after at least one approved line; 59% had already had Lu-177 dotatate.
39282913.bottom_line: CABINET establishes that cabozantinib has real activity after Lu-177 dotatate and targeted therapy, where nothing was previously established, more than doubling progression-free survival in both cohorts (8.4 against 3.9 months extrapancreatic, 13.8 against 4.4 months pancreatic) by blinded central review. It establishes nothing about survival, with hazard ratios of 0.86 and 0.95 and crossover in a third to a half of the placebo arms, and nothing about how patients feel, since quality of life was unchanged while two thirds needed dose reduction to a median of about 38 mg and a third of the extrapancreatic arm stopped for toxicity. The trial was also stopped early on local rather than central assessments, so the decision to terminate was taken on a different endpoint from the one reported, and the comparator was placebo, leaving cabozantinib untested against chemotherapy or any other tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
39282913.funding: Supported by grants from the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health (U10CA180821 and U10CA180882 to the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology, U10CA180820 to ECOG-ACRIN, U10CA180868 to NRG Oncology, U10CA180888 to SWOG, and UG1CA189856, UG1CA232760, UG1CA233180, UG1CA233290, UG1CA233329 and UG1CA233331) and by Exelixis, the manufacturer of cabozantinib. Individual disclosure forms were filed with the journal rather than printed in the article.

limitations: The recommendations preferring RLT over targeted agents and over chemotherapy rest on cross-trial comparison and retrospective series rather than head-to-head data, which the panel reflects in grades of 2b - B and 3b - A, and it notes that COMPETE and COMPOSE are still running.
The G2-G3 recommendation is written in anticipation of a regulatory approval that had not yet occurred, hence the phrasing 'once approved'.
The frail-patient recommendation is graded level 5, that is expert opinion, and rests on a single retrospective matched cohort.

The literature search was deliberately restricted to 177Lu-DOTATATE, so the document cannot speak to 90Y-DOTATOC or newer radioligands, nor to the intra-arterial and combination strategies it mentions.

The panel sets out the limits of RECIST 1.1 in this disease at length: these tumours may stabilise or even enlarge while responding, central necrosis during RLT produces false-positive size increases, and shrinkage can be delayed, so RECIST should be applied cautiously in slow-growing GEP-NET.

The Choi criteria perform equally or markedly better in published comparisons but rely on portal venous phase images while arterial phase is standard for these vascular tumours, which the panel calls a major limitation on using Choi in the neuroendocrine context.
Chemotherapy is retained as the choice for pancreatic NET with high tumour burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, a carve-out from the panel's own recommendation to prefer RLT.
critique: The grading does not track the evidence. The recommendation to prefer radioligand therapy over chemotherapy is given the document's strongest recommendation grade (A) on one of its weakest evidence levels (3b), while the recommendation to prefer it over everolimus or sunitinib carries better evidence (2b) and a weaker grade (B). A reader cannot tell what the letters mean.

The central second-line recommendation is built from a 508-patient matched retrospective series (progression-free survival 2.2 against 0.6 years) and a phase 2 trial in pancreatic NET (OCLURANDOM, 12-month progression-free survival 80.5% against 42%). No randomised head-to-head comparison of radioligand therapy against everolimus, sunitinib or chemotherapy existed when this was written, and the document's own grades concede it.

Early incorporation of radioligand therapy is recommended at the document's highest level, 1b - A, on the reasoning that high tumour burden reduces its efficacy. That is a prognostic observation. No trial randomised early against delayed radioligand therapy, so the strength of this recommendation is not supported by the kind of evidence a 1b label implies.

Pre-committing to a recommendation 'once approved' leaves practice tied to a regulatory decision, and the trial behind it does not match the recommendation's scope. NETTER-2 enrolled newly diagnosed patients with no documented progression, required uptake score 3 or 4 in every target lesion, capped Ki-67 at 55% and excluded anyone with prior hepatic embolisation or ablation, none of which qualifies the statement here.

There is no surgical or liver-directed content whatever. Locoregional therapy appears only as something to be excluded on pre-RLT imaging, and the document says nothing about debulking, embolisation, radioembolisation or sequencing in liver-dominant disease, although hepatic tumour burden is the very variable it invokes to argue for treating early.

The retreatment recommendation rests on a confounded observation. Patients who reached a cumulative renal absorbed dose of 23 Gy had nearly double the median progression-free and overall survival, but reaching a higher cumulative dose requires surviving and tolerating more cycles, so the association is in part a consequence of doing well rather than a cause of it.
Dosimetry is invoked to tailor the retreatment dose and no dosimetry protocol, renal constraint beyond the 23 Gy figure, or marrow constraint is specified anywhere.

The method is thin for a document of this reach. Ten questions, a MEDLINE search whose dates and search strings are not reported in the body, grades assigned by the panel itself, and no independent evidence review, no external review and no voting or agreement statistic described.
A level 5 recommendation, that is pure expert opinion, is given strength B for treating frail patients, a combination the grading framework the panel invokes does not support.

Seven named authors declare consultancy or speaker honoraria from Advanced Accelerator Applications, Novartis, ITM, Ipsen, Recordati, Advanz, Harpoon Therapeutics, Merck or Harbour Biomedical, and the document's single most consequential output is a recommendation to prefer those companies' radioligand over competing drug classes.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so a set of recommendations that reorders second-line therapy for this disease entered the literature without external appraisal.
39395114.n: No patient cohort. A four-society Italian panel answered ten predefined questions from a MEDLINE search restricted to 177Lu-DOTATATE plus expert opinion, assigning each statement a level of evidence (1 to 5) and a strength of recommendation (A to D).
39395114.bottom_line: This four-society Italian consensus moves radioligand therapy to second line in somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NET, ahead of high-dose somatostatin analogue, everolimus, sunitinib and chemotherapy, and recommends incorporating it early on the grounds that high tumour burden reduces its efficacy. Only the comparison with high-dose somatostatin analogue rests on randomised evidence; preference over targeted agents comes from one phase 2 trial and preference over chemotherapy from a matched retrospective series, which the panel itself grades 2b and 3b while attaching strength A to the weaker of the two. The document is silent on surgery and liver-directed therapy, mentioning locoregional treatment only as something to exclude on pre-treatment imaging, so it cannot be used to decide between radioligand therapy and debulking or embolisation in liver-dominant disease.
39395114.funding: Open access funding provided by Universita degli Studi di Roma La Sapienza within the CRUI-CARE Agreement; no study funding is declared. Seven named authors declare consultancy or speaker honoraria outside the submitted work from Advanced Accelerator Applications, Novartis, ITM, Ipsen, Recordati, Advanz, Harpoon Therapeutics, Merck and Harbour Biomedical; the remaining authors declare no conflict of interest.

limitations: A prospectively collected trial cohort is compared with a retrospective PRRT-only cohort.
The PRRT-only cohort suffered from reporting bias, which forced the authors to drop the toxicity analysis and the analysis of hormone-related complaints altogether.
Heterogeneity of the primary tumours made propensity-score matching difficult and limited it to 1:1, and even with restrictive inclusion and matching criteria an imbalance in ECOG score remained.
No patient in the combination cohort had received prior chemotherapy against 21% of the PRRT-only cohort, an imbalance that could not be entered into the propensity model.

The finding that every combination-cohort patient rose at least one ECOG point after PRRT is described as striking, and the authors caution that it may reflect less rigorous retrospective data collection rather than a real difference.
Too few patients had liver-only disease to run the separate analysis that would most support the hypothesis, so no solid evidence is offered for the population the authors think would benefit most.
The gastrointestinal versus pancreatic subgroup difference rests on very small numbers and the authors say it warrants confirmation.
There is no clear definition of liver-dominant disease in the literature or in any guideline, which the authors identify as a basic obstacle to positioning SIRT at all.
Concerns about long-term hepatotoxicity rest on small retrospective studies describing pseudo-cirrhotic imaging morphology whose clinical implications remain unknown.
Short-term quality of life is not hampered by SIRT but long-term quality-of-life effects remain unknown, and no quality-of-life data were collected here.

All available SIRT data in NET, including this study, use a one-size-fits-all fixed activity; the authors state that personalised dosimetry is now standard elsewhere and that prospective dosimetry studies are needed.
critique: The primary endpoint is reported as two proportions with heavily overlapping confidence intervals and no between-group test at all: 68% (95% CI 43-87) against 55% (32-76). No hazard ratio and no p value is given for the primary comparison, and the same is true of the hepatic PFS figures (82%, 57-96 against 50%, 28-72) on which the conclusion actually rests.

After matching, the arm receiving the extra liver-directed treatment had less liver disease, not more. Median liver tumour burden was 8% in the combination cohort against 20% in the PRRT-only cohort (6% against 13% at the 3-month scan), even though fractional liver involvement at 3 months was one of the ten covariates in the final propensity model, and even though the whole rationale of the study is bulky hepatic disease.

Both arms are given a guaranteed event-free run-in. Patients who progressed by RECIST at the 3-month scan after the last PRRT cycle were removed, while progression-free survival is measured from the first PRRT cycle, so roughly nine months of PRRT plus three months of restaging are credited to every patient before an event can be recorded.

How many patients that exclusion removed from each matched arm cannot be worked out. The text gives 4 (13%) in the combination cohort and 16 (18%) in the PRRT-only cohort and cites Table 2, which presents the matched sets of 24, yet 16 of 24 would be 67%; the percentages belong to the full analysis sets and the matched-set figures are never stated.

The ECOG imbalance the authors could not match on is the strongest evidence that the two cohorts were observed differently rather than being clinically different. Performance status was balanced before PRRT and then diverged completely afterwards, with 0% of the combination cohort and 75% of the controls at ECOG 0, which is what prospective trial monitoring against retrospective chart abstraction would produce. The paper acknowledges the possibility and then uses the same observation to argue that its treated cohort was the sicker one.

The argument that the combination cohort had worse prognosis is assembled selectively. More pulmonary metastases are cited as adverse, fewer bone metastases are noted as pointing the other way, extrahepatic disease differed in the full analysis set (83% versus 64%) but was balanced after matching (88% in both), and less liver disease is not mentioned in that passage at all.

Matching discards most of the control pool. Ninety PRRT-only patients were collected and 24 used, with a ten-covariate logistic propensity model fitted across 120 patients to produce those pairs, and no overlap or common-support diagnostics are reported beyond a balance figure.

The combination cohort is defined by having completed and tolerated four full cycles of PRRT and then being fit enough for radioembolisation within 20 weeks. Being alive, non-progressing and well enough for a second procedure is an eligibility requirement in one arm and not the other, however carefully the controls are matched on baseline covariates.

The subgroup numbers do not agree between the results and the discussion. The gastrointestinal and pancreatic subgroups are given as n=10 versus 14 and n=6 versus 7 in the results, and as n=13 versus 15 and n=8 versus 7 in the discussion, for the single finding the paper describes as most interesting.

The benefit is hepatic and the endpoints that matter clinically are unchanged. Median PFS was 30.8 against 30.3 months and median hepatic PFS 33.5 against 30.3 months, with no overall survival difference, so the case for adding SIRT rests entirely on two-year landmark proportions and on a response rate measured in the organ that was irradiated.

Best objective response is the softest available endpoint for this comparison. Radioembolisation produces necrosis and cavitation in treated lesions, and a 71% versus 25% response rate measured by RECIST size change in an irradiated liver cannot be separated from the direct physical effect of the treatment on the target lesions.

No dosimetry of any kind is reported: no absorbed dose to tumour or to normal liver, no dose-volume metrics, in a study of two sequential radiation treatments to the same organ. The authors raise the point themselves as a general deficiency of the field, having run their own study the same way.

The two analyses a clinician would most want, toxicity and hormonal symptom control, were abandoned because the retrospective arm's records would not support them. A combination of two radiation therapies is therefore recommended as safe and feasible on the basis of a comparison in which safety could not be compared.

The funder manufactures the product. The study is funded by Terumo, which makes the holmium-166 microspheres, two co-authors are employed by Medical Affairs Interventional Oncology at Terumo Europe NV and a third is from a commercial biostatistics company, and the conflict-of-interest statement reads that the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so this propensity-matched comparison of a single-arm trial against a historical cohort entered the literature without independent appraisal.
40302310.n: 24 matched pairs: the 30 patients of the prospective single-arm HEPAR PLuS phase 2 trial set against 90 PRRT-only patients collected retrospectively from four European ENETS Centres of Excellence, reduced to 1:1 matching on a ten-covariate propensity score.
40302310.bottom_line: This suggests that adding holmium-166 radioembolisation after four cycles of 177Lu-DOTATATE improves control of liver disease, with two-year hepatic progression-free survival of 82% against 50% and an intrahepatic response rate of 75% against 29% in 24 matched pairs. It does not establish benefit: the primary endpoint is two proportions with overlapping confidence intervals and no statistical test, median PFS and overall survival are unchanged, the combination arm had less liver disease after matching (8% against 20% burden) despite bulky disease being the rationale, and toxicity could not be compared at all. The one arm is a prospective trial cohort that had to survive and tolerate full PRRT to qualify, the other a retrospective chart series, and the study is funded by the microsphere manufacturer with two of its employees as co-authors under a declaration of no conflicts.
